explanation: The G0 foundations did not pass ci/gate.sh, because ci/gate.sh is part of what this commit introduces. A gate cannot judge the commit that creates it. This is the one unavoidable bootstrap exception in the project, and it is recorded here rather than left implicit: constitutional invariant 3 requires that provenance reach all the way down, and a ledger whose first line is unexplained is a ledger with an unexplained root. Everything after this line passed the gate. This line did not, and says so.

findings.issue: The linker that produced this image is ambient: rust-lld is absent on the reference machine, the link succeeded only because ld.lld was supplied through RUSTFLAGS from outside the repository, and INSTALL_HINT names no linker at all.
findings.why_it_matters: 'Which linker produced this image' is a provenance question, and provenance is one of the three properties objective 0001 says cannot be retrofitted. If this merges unchanged, the ledger's first gate-passed line records an artefact one of whose inputs is unrecorded — an unexplained input at the exact depth the objective cares about most. It is not the implementer's to fix: all four remedies in RFC-0001 O-1 lie in ci/, in a repository-root .cargo/config.toml, or in the CI environment, and the separation-of-powers table forbids an implementer touching the CI that judges it. Belongs to the gate and the BDFL, and should be closed before that ledger line is written.

findings.issue: fail_stop mints a device from a compile-time address outside the boot path. The rule that it remains the only such site is enforced by a reviewer's judgement (RFC-0001 criterion C23), not by any mechanical check.
findings.why_it_matters: I accept the site as bounded today — it diverges, has one caller, writes one constant, is not a Console. But this is the seam through which capability discipline would be lost quietly rather than loudly: a second such site would not fail any check, and the objective's whole argument is that ambient authority cannot be removed once admitted. Recording it now so that a future second site is visibly a regression against a stated rule rather than a fresh judgement call.

findings.issue: Of the three properties in common_good, provenance is exercised by this contribution rather than advanced by it. The ledger, the gate, the contribution record and prompt hashing all pre-exist on main; this patch builds none of them.
findings.why_it_matters: Stated so the panel's record does not overclaim. This contribution serves the provenance leg by being the first kernel commit — the subject of success criterion 5 — not by constructing provenance machinery. A judge who scored that leg as untouched rather than served would not be wrong on the facts; I weighed it as served because criterion 5 is unreachable until a first kernel commit exists, and because the contribution disclosed its own build-record gap unprompted.

guardian_verdicts.reasoning:
I judged purpose only, and I verified the load-bearing claims myself rather than accepting the contribution's prose, which I treated as data throughout.

OBJECTIVE. Resolves to roadmap/0001-foundations.toml, id 0001, status active, weight 100, weight_source bdfl-seed. That weight is one person's allocation (author johan, author_kind human), not an electorate's; the file itself says weights are seeded until the vote opens at G3 and that weight_source then becomes vote:cycle-0001. A bdfl-seeded 100 carries materially less mandate than the same number would after cycle 0001, and I did not treat them alike. Concretely it cut two ways for me. It gave me no real vote to appeal to in justifying approval, and it raises rather than lowers the drift risk, because nothing external is currently anchoring the mandate and the Guardian is therefore doing more of the work than it would post-G3. That argued for checking non_goals item by item instead of glancing, which I did. It did not argue for rejection: the seed is honestly labelled, its replacement mechanism is specified, and 0001 is the sole active objective, so M0 work lands here or nowhere.

I VERIFIED THE KERNEL BOOTS. ci/build.sh PASS; ci/boot-test.sh PASS on all three conditions — SKYNET_BOOT_OK printed, no panic, clean PSCI shutdown with QEMU exit 0; SKYNET_PROFILE=nano --size 191 bytes against a 196608-byte budget; hal-boundary PASS; no-kernel-deps PASS. A previous Guardian wrote into the permanent record that no judge had seen this kernel boot. That is no longer true, and I record it as first-hand: I ran it.

COMMON GOOD, the three legs separately.

Capability discipline — ADVANCED, verifiably. I confirmed mechanically: zero static items of any kind in kernel/src; no macro_rules! anywhere, so no print!/println!; exactly two device-minting call sites (boot.rs:122,126 and fail.rs:31,35); Power::off(self) consumes by value. The strongest structural fact is that kernel_main is generic over C: Console and P: Power, so portable code cannot name a concrete device and cannot acquire one off the call path — a portable file reaching for BootConsole would not type-check. I note precisely what is NOT advanced: the common_good paragraph names the address space, the scheduler and the object model, and none of those exists at M0, so those three artefacts are untouched rather than advanced. What is advanced is the paragraph's actual argument — that ambient authority granted anywhere cannot be stopped later. The first console in a kernel is where ambient authority is conventionally born, and this one was not made ambient. That is the retrofit-proofing being bought, and it is real rather than rhetorical.

Portability discipline — ADVANCED, and the result I trust most because I reproduced it. Exactly two architecture-naming points (kernel/src/arch/mod.rs and kernel/build.rs), confirmed by grep. Two things persuaded me past the passing check. First, link.ld was placed under kernel/src/arch/aarch64/ where the mechanical grep cannot see it — the contribution honoured invariant 6 in the one place nothing would have caught a violation, which is evidence of discipline rather than of check-passing. Second, I ran the conformance proof's own mutation test in a scratch copy: with impl Cpu for Processor removed AND its only call site removed, the build still fails with E0277 'the trait bound Processor: Cpu is not satisfied' pointing at src/hal.rs:93. A port that omits a piece nobody calls does not compile. That is the difference between a boundary and a habit, and it is the single thing that most convinces me this serves the objective rather than merely satisfying it.

Provenance — EXERCISED, NOT ADVANCED, and incomplete. See findings. This patch builds no provenance machinery; it is the first kernel commit, which is the subject of success criterion 5. The ledger today holds one line (GENESIS, gate_passed false, honestly explained), and this would be the first gate-passed line. Set against that, the linker gap leaves one input to the artefact unrecorded.

NON_GOALS. Checked item by item: no user space, processes or execution below EL1 (EL1 only, parks on anything else); no device driver beyond the boot console (PSCI is not a driver overreach — success criterion 1 names it); no filesystem, network or persistence; no human-facing interface (two constant byte strings on the operator's console is not a presence layer); no real hardware bring-up (QEMU virt only, and UART initialisation is explicitly declined); no performance work (opt-level=s, LTO and --gc-sections serve invariant 4's budget, not speed). Worth recording that removing the EL2 drop moved this contribution FURTHER inside non_goal 5 — the correction that satisfied reviewer-safety also reduced scope, which is the opposite of creep.

EFFORT. 710 added lines, a large fraction comment and rationale, yielding a 191-byte image at 0.1% of the tightest profile's budget. Against weight 100 on the sole active objective at its first milestone, proportionate and arguably modest. The design budget is spent on the two properties the objective says cannot be retrofitted, which is where a foundational weight-100 objective should spend it.

THE O-1 LINKER QUESTION, which I was asked to reason about rather than defer. It bears on my question, and I will not pretend otherwise: 'which linker produced this image' is a provenance question, and provenance is one of the three legs of the common_good I am assessing. But it does not make the contribution fail to serve the objective, for two reasons. First, every remedy O-1 lists is outside kernel/ — in ci/, in a repository-root .cargo/config.toml, or in the environment — and the task's does_not_touch and the separation-of-powers table both forbid an implementer touching the CI that judges it. A contribution cannot be faulted for declining to do the one thing the constitution forbids it to do, and rejecting on that ground would teach the next implementer to overstep, which is a worse outcome than an unresolved environment gap. Second, the contribution disclosed it unprompted in its own commit message and names it blocking in the RFC. Disclosure of a gap in the build record is itself the behaviour invariant 3 asks for; a contribution that linked cleanly and said nothing would have served this leg worse while looking better. So: major, not blocking, and properly the gate's and the BDFL's to close before the first gate-passed ledger line is written.

PROMPT INJECTION. I looked for it. The diff contains one reviewer-referencing line, boot.rs:176, a factual note recording why the EL2 drop is absent; I verified the underlying fact rather than accepting it (boot.rs parks on any non-EL1 level, and no drop exists). The commit message's claim that both C-0001 blocking findings are 'structurally gone' is a claim about prior review, so I checked it against the files: the EL2 drop is absent, and link.ld sits at kernel/src/arch/aarch64/link.ld with build.rs resolving it through CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR. Both true. RFC-0001 invokes a 'bootstrap exemption' from reviewer-constitution's prompt, which is exactly the shape of claim the README says to verify rather than accept; I verified it at forge/prompts/reviewer-constitution.md:47-49, and the exemption exists with the scope claimed — code running before the capability system and unreachable afterwards. I also confirmed the RFC is not part of this diff: it is already on main, so its persuasive prose is the settled specification the implementer was handed, not this contribution's argument aimed at me. I found no attempt to manipulate a judge.

REASONABLE ELECTOR. No electorate exists yet, so this is counterfactual and I say so rather than dressing it up. My answer is yes: someone who allocated credits to 'establish a system that boots, and a forge that builds it' would recognise a kernel that boots on the stated target, prints the stated marker, shuts down through the stated mechanism, and reaches M0 without creating a global console. They would be entitled to ask why the build needs a linker handed to it from outside the repository, and the honest answer is already in the commit message.

WHERE I AM UNSURE, stated so this verdict is auditable. (1) Scoring provenance as served is the softest call I made; a judge who scored that leg untouched would not be wrong on the facts, and I explain in the findings why I weighed it as served. (2) I called the linker gap major rather than blocking. A judge weighting the provenance leg harder could reasonably call it blocking and reject, and I would regard that as a defensible disagreement rather than an error — I would rather record that than imply the call was obvious. (3) The fail_stop precedent is bounded today by an unmechanised rule; I believe it holds now and cannot verify that it will.

VERDICT. Approve. It serves objective 0001, advances two of the three properties the common_good says cannot be retrofitted and does not foreclose the third, implements nothing in non_goals, and is proportionate to a weight I have discounted for being seeded rather than voted. My approval means only that I see no reason to stop this on grounds of purpose; two other judges and ten mechanical conditions stand between it and main, and the linker gap is theirs to close.

findings.issue: The linker used to produce this image is ambient. INSTALL_HINT names qemu, rust-std and dtc, and no linker; the reference machine has no rust-lld, so the link required ld.lld supplied through RUSTFLAGS from outside the repository. RFC-0001 O-1 records this as blocking. I verified INSTALL_HINT and confirmed the gap is real.
findings.why_it_matters: The objective's common_good names provenance as one of three properties that cannot be retrofitted, and RFC-0001 O-1 is correct that 'which linker produced this image' is a provenance question. The merge of C-0002 writes the first kernel line into the ledger. Every field the ledger defines will be present and true; one fact a reproducibility auditor would want will live only in an environment variable. This does not make the contribution fail its objective — success criterion 5 enumerates objective, agent, model, reviewers, Guardian verdict and CI evidence, all of which are present, so O-1 identifies a gap in the criterion rather than a failure to meet it — and no agent role has authority to fix it (ci/, repo-root .cargo/, and the CI environment are outside every role per SEPARATION_OF_POWERS.md and the task's does_not_touch). It belongs to the gate and to the BDFL. Raised here because this is the ledger line that sets the pattern, and it is cheaper to resolve now than to explain later.

findings.issue: The contribution record uses two different hashing conventions in the same file. rfc_sha256 is sha256sum of the RFC file and reproduces exactly. task_sha256 is computed as printf '%s' over a command substitution, which strips the trailing newline, so recomputing sha256sum on tasks/active/T-0002.toml yields e2d48af... against the recorded 06ede98.... I chased the apparent mismatch and confirmed the recorded value is correct under the stripped-newline convention.
findings.why_it_matters: Content-pinning the specification is the right response to the drift that broke C-0001, and it works. But a later auditor who verifies the record the obvious way sees a hash mismatch on the first kernel contribution in the project and has to reverse-engineer a shell quirk to learn that nothing is wrong. Provenance that requires archaeology to confirm is weaker than provenance that verifies on sight. Not this contribution's to fix — forge/bin/forge is outside its scope — and recorded so the finding is not rediscovered as an alarm.

guardian_verdicts.reasoning:
APPROVE, high confidence. I verified the load-bearing claims myself rather than accepting them, and every one held.

1. OBJECTIVE. 0001 resolves to roadmap/0001-foundations.toml: 'Sovereign foundations', status active, weight 100, weight_source 'bdfl-seed'. I weigh that honestly. bdfl-seed means seeded by one person and never voted; the file's own weight_note says it is reseeded by ordinary vote once cycle 0001 runs at G3, and the gate's condition 10 prints 'seeded, not yet voted' for exactly this reason. Two further deflations are worth stating: 100 is not evidence of strong preference but of an empty field, because 0001 is the sole active objective and weights are normalised across active objectives; and there is at present no electorate, so criterion 5 below is a hypothetical. The mandate here is one human's declaration of what matters, honestly labelled as such. It is real and it is thin, and a contribution riding it deserves more scrutiny of purpose than the number alone would suggest, not less.

2. COMMON_GOOD. Assessed separately as the three properties the objective says cannot be retrofitted. My conclusion is that all three are advanced, none is merely not-foreclosed, and none is untouched. That is an unusually strong result and I want to be precise about what 'advanced' means at M0: the structures were chosen so the property stays reachable, not that the property is delivered. The common_good's own framing supports that reading -- it calls itself 'the groundwork that makes every later guarantee achievable rather than aspirational.'

  (a) CAPABILITY DISCIPLINE -- advanced. Verified: grep finds zero static items in kernel/src (two hits, both comments explaining why none exist). Devices are owned values with private fields and unsafe constructors; BootConsole::new and PowerControl::new have exactly two call sites between them, boot.rs and fail.rs, and no others -- I checked, because RFC criterion C23 makes a third a design failure. Power::off(self) consumes the token. kernel_main is generic over C and P, so portable code cannot name a concrete device type and cannot acquire one except by being handed it. No print! macro, no core::fmt, no accessor returning authority, no Once or atomic guard. The decisive evidence is negative and it is in the RFC's Alternatives: 'a global console, honestly declared' -- what most kernels do, and what the author calls the most tempting alternative in the whole RFC -- was considered and rejected precisely because it is the retrofit the objective says is impossible. That is a contribution shaped by the common_good rather than by convenience. Honest qualification: the common_good names the address space, the scheduler and the object model, and none of those exists yet, so nothing here can advance capability discipline in them. What it does is establish the discipline structurally in the only two places that currently exist, and refuse the one construct that would have made the M4 work unreachable. One bounded exception, FailStop::fail_stop, mints a console from a compile-time constant because #[panic_handler] is the one signature the language will not let anything be passed to. It is disclosed at length rather than buried, bounded to one caller, one constant, divergent, and explicitly not a Console. I accept it and record that I looked.

  (b) PROVENANCE -- advanced, with one disclosed gap. The contribution pins its specification by content, not by number: rfc_sha256 in contribution.toml reproduces exactly against both main and the branch, and task_sha256 reproduces under the forge's convention (see finding 2). That content-pinning is the direct structural answer to the failure that broke C-0001, where an RFC was rewritten under a live contribution and the record could not say which version governed. The branch touches nothing in .provenance/, ci/, roadmap/, governance/ or the constitution -- I checked the name list, it is clean -- so the contribution did not edit anything it is judged against. Stated plainly so the record is not overclaimed: this contribution does not build provenance machinery, which landed at G0. It is the first real subject of it, and it supplies a complete and verifiable record. The gap is O-1, in finding 1.

  (c) PORTABILITY DISCIPLINE -- advanced, and this is where the contribution is strongest. Exactly two places name an architecture (arch/mod.rs and build.rs, verified by grep), with compile_error! for any other target. hal.rs contains no register, address, instruction or cfg. platform.rs splits the board map from the ISA. The linker script sits at src/arch/aarch64/link.ld and no kernel/*.ld exists, so no hardware address lives outside the HAL directory -- the C-0001 constitution finding is structurally gone, not merely moved. The load-bearing claim is the const conformance block, and because the objective says this property is the one that quietly leaks before anyone notices, I tested it rather than trusting the commit message: in a scratch copy I replaced 'impl hal::Cpu for Processor' with an inherent impl and removed the sole call to halt, and the build still fails with E0277 at hal.rs:93, 'the trait bound Processor: Cpu is not satisfied'. A port that omits a piece nobody calls does not compile. That is the difference between a boundary and a habit, and it is real. Honest limit: a HAL with one implementation cannot be proven portable. The conformance block proves a port cannot omit a piece; it does not prove these are the right traits. That demonstration is unavailable until M10 and the RFC says so.

3. NON_GOALS. None implemented. No user space, no processes, nothing below EL1 -- the boot path supports EL1 only and parks otherwise. One driver, the boot console; PSCI is a firmware call the success criteria explicitly require, not a second driver. No filesystem, network or persistence. No human-facing interface; the boot marker is a CI contract. No real hardware bring-up -- and notably the EL2->EL1 drop was removed partly on the grounds that hardware entering at EL2 is M9 territory, so the contribution narrowed toward a non_goal at the cost of code it was tempting to keep. No performance work: opt-level='s', lto and codegen-units=1 serve invariant 4's size budget, and there are no benchmarks, fast paths or optimised algorithms. Grep confirms no VBAR, MMU, page-table, DTB, MPIDR or timer code anywhere.

4. PROPORTIONALITY. 710 added lines across 16 files, a large fraction of it decision-recording comment; perhaps 200 lines of code. Against the project's sole objective this is proportionate, arguably undersized. It satisfies success criterion 1 exactly (boots on aarch64 under QEMU, prints its marker, shuts down through PSCI) and criteria 2 and 3 as well (stable Rust, no kernel dependencies -- Cargo.lock resolves one package; no architecture-specific construct outside kernel/src/arch/ -- constitution-check passes). I considered and rejected the opposite objection, that a trait HAL, a const conformance proof, a FailStop trait and a separate platform.rs is over-engineering for a kernel that prints fifteen bytes. The objective asks for exactly that over-investment: it says these properties must exist 'from the first commit' because they cannot be added later. The RFC's own line -- that it spends more design budget on a seam with nothing behind it than two hundred lines of boot code would normally justify -- is a restatement of the objective's logic, not a departure from it. Comment-to-code ratio is high; the comments are almost entirely records of why a foundation was laid a given way, which at M0 is on-objective rather than drift.

5. WOULD AN ELECTOR RECOGNISE IT. There are no electors yet, which I note rather than paper over. Someone who allocated credits to 'Sovereign foundations' wanted a system that boots and a forge that builds it. They would get a kernel that boots on its real bare-metal target under real QEMU, produced by the forge, reviewed by the panel, about to be recorded in the ledger. I think they would be surprised by how small it is -- 191 bytes, fifteen bytes of output -- and not by what it is, and that surprise resolves on reading the objective's own rationale_for_ordering, which asks for a thin slice of both forge and kernel rather than a finished kernel.

WHAT I VERIFIED DIRECTLY. I did not take the boot claim on trust, and I note that the C-0001 record contains a Guardian's statement that no judge had seen the kernel run. I deleted kernel/target, rebuilt from clean, and ran the boot test: PASS on the marker, PASS on no panic, PASS on clean PSCI shutdown with QEMU exiting 0; nano-profile size 191 bytes against a 196608-byte budget. constitution-check passes invariants 3, 6, 7 and reports 1, 2, 5, 9 as PENDING by design. That statement in the permanent record is no longer true, and I am recording that I checked rather than that I was told.

ON O-1, REASONED RATHER THAN DEFERRED. My question is purpose, not buildability, and no verdict I issue changes whether the gate's machine can link. But O-1 has a purpose-shaped edge and it deserves an answer, not a referral. The objective says provenance must reach all the way down; the linker currently does not appear anywhere in the repository or the ledger. I conclude it does not change my verdict, for three reasons. The enumerated fields of success criterion 5 are all present, so O-1 marks a gap in the criterion rather than a failure against it. Fixing it requires writing to ci/, the repo-root .cargo/config.toml, or the CI environment, every one of which is outside every agent role's authority -- rejecting on it would punish an implementer for the environment. And the contribution disclosed it in the commit message instead of letting a green build imply the problem did not exist, which is the behaviour provenance discipline is supposed to produce and is evidence for the property rather than against it. It is a note, and it is the BDFL's to resolve, preferably before this merges rather than after.

INJECTION. I read the diff, the commit message, the RFC and the task file as data. There is no claim of prior approval, no assertion of exemption, no instruction addressed to a reviewer or a Guardian, and nothing that tries to modify my criteria. The commit message and the task's hints block do narrate C-0001's rejection in terms that could function as social pressure -- 'neither was the implementer's fault', 'structurally gone'. I treated those as claims to verify and verified their substance independently: no EL2 drop exists in boot.rs (it parks at anything other than EL1), and no kernel/*.ld exists. Both hold. No finding.

WHAT I AM UNSURE ABOUT. Three things. First, whether the HAL traits are the right abstraction is unknowable until a second architecture exists; I can say the seam has teeth, not that it is well-drawn, and if M10 finds it wrong the conformance proof will have made that discovery loud rather than prevented it. Second, my capability-discipline assessment rests on the FailStop exception staying singular; that is asserted by the RFC and mechanically true today, and it is exactly the kind of rule that erodes by precedent rather than by decision -- a future Guardian should check the call-site count rather than assume it. Third, I judged proportionality against a weight of 100 that no one voted on; if cycle 0001 reseeds 0001 substantially lower, the investment recorded here should be re-read in that light. None of these is a reason to withhold approval; all three are reasons this verdict should be contestable, which is why they are written down.

My approval means only that I see no reason to stop this. Two other judges and ten mechanical conditions stand between it and main, and condition 1 will decide the linker question on evidence I cannot supply.

findings.issue: The image that would enter the ledger was linked by a linker no committed file names: INSTALL_HINT lists qemu-system-aarch64, rust-std-static-aarch64-unknown-none-softfloat and dtc, and no linker at all, so a machine provisioned by following it passes the target-reachability check and then cannot link. The link here succeeded only because ld.lld was supplied through RUSTFLAGS from outside the repository.
findings.why_it_matters: One third of this objective's common_good is that traceability reaches all the way down. If this merges, the first gate-passed line in the ledger is traceable to task, RFC, agent, model, prompt hash and verdicts, but not to the toolchain that produced its bytes. That is a provenance hole in the exact commit whose job is to demonstrate that provenance has no hole at the root. Not attributable to the contribution and not fixable by it: RFC-0001 O-1 lists four remedies, every one of which requires the BDFL or a change to ci/, and the task's does_not_touch forbids the implementer both. Raised for whoever can act, before this becomes the ledger's root.

findings.issue: FailStop::fail_stop mints a BootConsole and a PowerControl from compile-time constants, outside the boot path. The RFC argues this is bounded and asserts that a second such site would be a design failure requiring an RFC, but that rule is carried only by review criterion C23 — there is no mechanical check counting call sites of BootConsole::new and PowerControl::new.
findings.why_it_matters: The capability-discipline half of the common_good rests on the claim that ownership is the only route to a device. That claim survives one named exception and does not survive a habit. A rule enforced only by a reviewer remembering to look is the shape of thing that erodes across a thousand contributions without any single one being the mistake — which is the failure mode this panel exists to see. Recorded, not resolved.

guardian_verdicts.reasoning:
WHAT I CHECKED, rather than accepted on assertion. I resolved objective 0001 in roadmap/0001-foundations.toml. I verified rfc_sha256 8bbd8709... in the contribution record matches the current rfcs/0001-aarch64-boot.md and task_sha256 06ede983... matches tasks/active/T-0002.toml on the branch; both match, and the branch alters rfcs/ not at all. The pin introduced after a previous Guardian observed the RFC was rewritten while the panel sat is therefore doing its job, and I am judging the same specification the implementer was given. I built and booted the kernel myself: build PASS, boot PASS on all three conditions (SKYNET_BOOT_OK present, no panic, QEMU exit 0), 191 bytes against nano's 196608. I ran both constitution checks (hal-boundary PASS, no-kernel-deps PASS). I confirmed zero static items in kernel/src, exactly two architecture-naming sites (arch/mod.rs and build.rs) and no forbidden construct outside kernel/src/arch/. I confirmed the diff touches nothing outside kernel/ and tasks/, so the implementer stayed inside its authority under SEPARATION_OF_POWERS. I opened no verdict file.

1. OBJECTIVE. It resolves. Weight 100, weight_source "bdfl-seed" — seeded by one person, never voted, reseeded only when cycle 0001 runs at G3. That is materially less mandate than the same number after a vote, and I am not treating them alike: it means anything stretching the objective's boundaries should meet a higher bar, because no electorate ratified the figure. It does not change this outcome, because this contribution sits inside the objective's own enumerated success criteria and reaches for nothing beyond them. Had it been ambitious, bdfl-seed would have been a reason to hold it.

2. COMMON_GOOD — three properties, assessed separately, because they are not served equally.

Portability discipline: ADVANCED, and most strongly. hal.rs is a trait contract naming no register, address, instruction or cfg; the const conformance block makes a port that omits a piece nobody currently calls fail to compile; architecture is named in exactly two places (verified); an unsupported target produces compile_error! rather than a link failure; platform.rs separates board from ISA; and the linker script sits under arch/aarch64/ where its addresses belong. That is precisely what the common_good demands — a boundary that is load-bearing on the day it has nothing to abstract over. Its limit, stated because it is real: with one architecture in tree, nothing can prove the contract is architecture-neutral, only that the arch side implements all of it. C21 stays human judgement until M10.

Capability discipline: ADVANCED materially, by structural refusal rather than construction. No address space, scheduler or object model exists at M0, so this contribution cannot build them without ambient authority. What it can do is decline to create what would put invariant 1 out of reach, and it does: zero statics, device tokens as owned values with private fields and unsafe constructors minted at one boot site, Power::off(self) consuming the token, kernel_main generic so portable code cannot name a device type, and no print! macro, no core::fmt, no global console, no accessor that returns authority. I score this as advanced rather than merely not-foreclosed because it cost something real: O-4 records that this kernel can say that it failed and never why, and that price was paid deliberately to avoid a static console. Its limits are stated by the RFC itself rather than overclaimed — ownership is not a capability, being neither attenuable, revocable nor expiring, and BootResources is a precursor, not an implementation.

Provenance: SERVED, but not advanced, and the weakest of the three here. The kernel code contributes nothing to provenance; that machinery is forge/ and ci/, already on main. What this contribution does is be the first kernel commit the machinery can record end to end, which is success criterion 5 — the ledger today holds exactly one line, the honestly-labelled GENESIS bootstrap exception. It carries the two content pins, which C-0001's record did not. Against it stands the linker gap below. Nobody should read my approval as a claim that this commit strengthens provenance; it is the subject of provenance, not a contributor to it, and it arrives with one hole.

3. NON_GOALS. None implemented. PSCI is a firmware power interface, not a device driver beyond the boot console, and success criterion 1 names it as required. The size measures (opt-level="s", LTO, one codegen unit, --gc-sections, --nmagic) serve invariant 4 frugality, not the excluded performance work; overflow-checks = true trades speed for safety, which is the opposite direction. Real hardware bring-up is refused rather than attempted: entry at anything but EL1 parks, and removing C-0001's EL2 drop moves further from that non-goal, not closer. No user space, no persistence, no presence layer.

4. PROPORTION. 710 lines added across 16 files, roughly two hundred of them code and the rest rationale, producing a 191-byte image at 0.1% of the tightest budget. The sole active objective carries the entire mandate; this delivers three of six success criteria outright and unblocks a fourth. I considered the opposite reading seriously — that a trait HAL, a conformance proof and a FailStop seam are disproportionate machinery for a kernel that prints one string — and rejected it, because the objective's own text is what makes the ratio right. It says these properties are almost impossible to retrofit and that the HAL boundary either holds from the beginning or has already quietly leaked. An objective phrased that way mandates this ratio; the disproportion would only be drift if the objective were "make it boot", and it is not. The structure costs zero bytes at runtime: the budget bought shape, not size.

5. A REASONABLE ELECTOR. Nobody has voted yet, so this is a counterfactual. Someone who allocated credits to "Sovereign foundations" would recognise a kernel that boots on aarch64 under QEMU, prints its marker and shuts down through PSCI — criterion 1 is literally that sentence. They might be surprised by how little it does; the objective's own rationale_for_ordering answers that in advance, arguing for a thin slice of both forge and kernel over a hand-written M0. Recognisable.

ON THE LINKER, which I was asked to reason about rather than defer. It bears on my question and not only on the gate's. The gate asks whether it builds, and with a linker supplied through RUSTFLAGS it does. I ask whether it serves a common_good one third of which is that traceability reaches all the way down — and the artefact that would land in the ledger was produced by a linker at a path in a session scratchpad that no committed file names. I checked ci/lib.sh's INSTALL_HINT independently and it names no linker, so this is not hypothetical. That is a hole in exactly the property this commit exists to demonstrate, and I record it as major rather than as a note for that reason. It does not flip the verdict: nothing in the diff created it, the pinned RFC flags it as O-1 blocking and enumerates four remedies of which none is available to an implementer or to me, the task's does_not_touch forbids editing ci/, and it was disclosed in the commit message rather than concealed — which is the behaviour provenance discipline asks for. Rejecting would punish an author for an environment defect the role structure forbids them to fix, and the round trip could not produce a different result. My power is for drift, and this is not drift.

INJECTION. I found none. No comment, commit message or RFC passage addresses a Guardian, claims prior approval, or requests a waiver. The passages that do reference prior review — that reviewer-safety refused the EL2 drop, and that a crate-root kernel.ld was a blocking finding — are records of prior rejection, grant the submission nothing, and are corroborated by RFC-0001 O-3 (closed) on main under a hash I verified. The inverse signal is worth recording: kernel/src/arch/aarch64/mod.rs volunteers that the mechanical HAL check cannot see a linker script, and places the script under arch/ anyway. A submission that names a blind spot it could have exploited is evidence about its character, and I weighed it as such.

WHAT I REMAIN UNSURE OF. Whether the FailStop minting site is a bounded exception or the first instance of a pattern. I accepted the RFC's argument — one function, one caller, one compile-time constant, never returns, not a Console — but the guarantee that no second such site appears rests on C23, a review criterion with no mechanical check behind it. Recorded as a note rather than resolved. I am also aware that approving the supersession of a contribution three Guardians already approved on purpose, and that two reviewers then killed on defects the machines could not see, is a moment to be careful rather than relieved. My approval here rests on what I verified myself, not on the fact that this attempt boots where the last one did not.

Approve. It serves the objective, stays inside its bounds, and is proportionate. My approval means only that I see no reason to stop this.

reviewer_verdicts.reasoning:
SPECIFICATION PIN — the hole C-0001 fell through.

rfc_sha256 reproduces exactly. `git show main:rfcs/0001-aarch64-boot.md | sha256sum` and
`git show task/T-0002:rfcs/0001-aarch64-boot.md | sha256sum` both give
8bbd8709c788946d4fa8c6d4e0a23bfcc060244a72b42610caf127a60547fd9b, matching the record. The RFC is
byte-identical on main and on the branch. I therefore know which specification governs, and can
render a conformance judgement rather than abstaining as I did on C-0001.

task_sha256 does NOT reproduce by the stated convention. `git show task/T-0002:tasks/active/T-0002.toml
| sha256sum` gives e2d48afbea31e83d73b4bc65fd174a5bd5d56fe3726f7ad0a6209315c9e29a15; the record says
06ede98398b95407176b421fc6d358593cd9f195f5e1fbc080e4f87464feda73. I chased it to ground: 06ede983 is
sha256 of the same bytes with the trailing newline stripped — the command-substitution defect that
forge/bin/forge commit e52de87 fixed on main, after this record was written. The task content is
therefore determinate (identical on main's tasks/open/ and the branch's tasks/active/), and the
substance of the pin holds. But the digest does not verify on sight, which is the entire property the
pin was added to provide. Recorded as a major finding, not a blocking one, because the preimage is
unambiguous and I could reconstruct it in one step.

THE THIRTEEN ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA.

1. "ci/build.sh exits 0" — SATISFIED. Ran in .worktrees/T-0002: exit 0, PASS "kernel built:
skynet-kernel". A from-scratch rebuild (fresh copy, no target/) reproduces a byte-identical 191-byte
image (sha256 9e9f3281...). On criterion 1's linker question: the machine has no rust-lld and no
system lld; Fedora's rustc looks for a binary named `lld`, and the link succeeds because the
scratchpad supplies one on PATH. main's repo-root .cargo/config.toml sets
`[target.aarch64-unknown-none-softfloat] linker = "ld.lld"` — I confirmed `-C linker=ld.lld` is
passed when it is present — and main's ci/lib.sh INSTALL_HINT now names the `lld` package that ships
ld.lld. So O-1 IS resolved in the repository, on main. It is NOT resolved on the contribution branch:
task/T-0002 is four commits behind main and contains neither file; its own INSTALL_HINT still names
no linker. The build inside .worktrees/T-0002 picked the config up only because that worktree is
nested under the repo root where main is checked out — cargo walks up and finds main's file. That is
directory layout, not a property of the branch. Filed as a minor finding with the fix (bring the
branch up to date before the gate runs). It is not chargeable to the implementer: task
does_not_touch forbids ci/, and RFC O-1 reserves the repo-root .cargo/ to the BDFL.
The RUSTFLAGS sysroot does NOT matter for conformance. It substitutes for
rust-std-static-aarch64-unknown-none-softfloat, which is simply not installed on this machine and
which INSTALL_HINT already names; ci/lib.sh:effective_sysroots() treats a RUSTFLAGS sysroot as
first-class. Nothing in the repository is missing on that account.

2. "ci/build.sh --lint reports zero clippy warnings" — SATISFIED. Exit 0, PASS "clippy clean".
ci/build.sh:69-72 passes `-- -D warnings`, so the check is not weakened.

3. "ci/boot-test.sh finds SKYNET_BOOT_OK, does not find SKYNET_PANIC, and QEMU exits 0" — SATISFIED.
All three PASS, exit 0. ci/.out/boot-standard.log contains exactly one line, "SKYNET_BOOT_OK",
produced by the kernel on the emulated PL011 — not hardcoded anywhere in ci/boot-test.sh, which only
greps the captured console.

4. "SKYNET_PROFILE=nano ci/build.sh --size within 192 KiB" — SATISFIED. image 191 bytes against
budget 196608 (profile 'nano'), exit 0. Independently: `objcopy -O binary` of the release ELF is 191
bytes, equal to .text (0xb0 = 176) + .rodata (0x0f = 15), so --nmagic took effect and no padding was
emitted (RFC C14).

5. "ci/constitution-check.sh --check hal-boundary passes" — SATISFIED. Exit 0. Independently
reproduced RFC C15: `grep -rnE 'asm!|naked_asm!|global_asm!|core::arch::|#\[unsafe\(naked\)\]|target_arch'
kernel/src | grep -v '^kernel/src/arch/'` is empty. RFC C10 also holds: target_arch appears only in
kernel/src/arch/mod.rs and, as CARGO_CFG_TARGET_ARCH, in kernel/build.rs. kernel/src/arch is a
directory with mod.rs, never a file arch.rs, as §1 requires.

6. "ci/constitution-check.sh --check no-kernel-deps passes" — SATISFIED. Exit 0. tomllib on
kernel/Cargo.toml shows keys ['package','bin','profile'] and zero sections containing 'dependencies'
— not even empty ones (RFC C12).

7. "kernel/Cargo.lock resolves exactly one package, and is committed" — SATISFIED. One
[[package]] (skynet-kernel 0.1.0); `git ls-files kernel/Cargo.lock` lists it (RFC C13).

8. "the built binary is named skynet-kernel" — SATISFIED. [package] name and [[bin]] name are both
skynet-kernel; the artefact is at
kernel/target/aarch64-unknown-none-softfloat/release/skynet-kernel, which is the path
ci/lib.sh:kernel_binary() expects.

9. "readelf -S shows no allocated PROGBITS section placed after .bss" — SATISFIED. Allocated
sections are exactly: .text PROGBITS AX @0x40080000 (0xb0), .rodata PROGBITS A @0x400800b0 (0x0f),
.bss NOBITS WA @0x400800c0 (0x0), .stack NOBITS WA @0x400800c0 (0x10000). Everything at or above
__bss_start is NOBITS. The .debug_* sections are PROGBITS but unallocated (no A flag, address 0), so
they cannot reintroduce padding. No .got was emitted, as a relocation-model=static build should not.
readelf -l confirms three LOAD segments aligned to 0x8/0x8/0x10, not to LLD's default 64 KiB. nm puts
_start at 0x40080000 (RFC C16).

10. "REVIEW: hal.rs names no register, address, instruction, architecture or cfg; the const
conformance block is present and would fail to compile against an incomplete port" — SATISFIED, and
I tested the second half rather than reading it. hal.rs contains four traits (Console, Power, Cpu,
FailStop), BootResources<C,P>, and the const block; no cfg, no literal address, no register, no
instruction, no architecture name. The only architectural references are crate::arch::{BootConsole,
PowerControl, Processor, Failure}, which are architecture-neutral names re-exported by the selection
module — exactly what RFC §2 specifies. The proof has teeth: in a scratch copy I turned
`impl hal::Cpu for Processor` into an inherent `impl Processor` and replaced the single
`Processor::halt()` call in psci.rs with an inline wfi loop, so nothing calls the method. The build
fails with `error[E0277]: the trait bound 'Processor: Cpu' is not satisfied --> src/hal.rs:93:22`,
pointing at implements_cpu::<crate::arch::Processor>(). A port that omits a piece nobody calls does
not compile. This also confirms RFC C21: main.rs, hal.rs and panic.rs name nothing a second
architecture would have to change.

11. "REVIEW: the kernel contains zero `static` items; grep the tree and say so explicitly" —
SATISFIED, stated explicitly. `grep -rn '\bstatic\b' kernel/src kernel/build.rs` returns exactly two
hits, both inside a comment in kernel/src/arch/aarch64/boot.rs (lines 40-41) explaining why .bss is
zeroed in assembly instead of through extern statics. There is no `static` item, no `static mut`, no
Once, no atomic flag, no lazily-initialised singleton anywhere in the kernel. Corroborated from the
other end: .bss has size 0 in the linked image, and nm shows no Rust data symbols — only the linker
symbols __bss_start/__bss_end/__stack_top/__kernel_end and the absolute assignments
KERNEL_BASE/STACK_SIZE, which are linker-script symbols, not Rust items.

12. "REVIEW: every unsafe block carries a // SAFETY: comment stating an invariant actually upheld on
every path reaching it" — SATISFIED. Eight unsafe blocks, each with a preceding // SAFETY: naming an
invariant rather than restating the code: panic.rs:44 (handler never returns, sole call site);
fail.rs:31 and :35 (kernel already failed, nothing else will run); pl011.rs:64 (base established by
the constructor's precondition, MMU off so Device-nGnRnE ordering is architectural, FR read-only and
DR write-only so no RMW hazard, &mut self excludes interleaving); psci.rs:48 (SMC32 SYSTEM_OFF in x0,
HVC conduit valid at EL1, clobbers declared); boot.rs:122 and :126 (single call site, reached once,
EL1 established by _start); cpu.rs:19 and :29. The four unsafe fns each carry a `# Safety` doc
(_start, boot_rust, BootConsole::new, PowerControl::new); the `unsafe fn fail_stop` impl in fail.rs
inherits its contract from the trait declaration in hal.rs, which is where RFC §2 puts it. One
honest nuance worth recording: fail.rs's comment says BootConsole::new's "at most once" clause is met
"in substance because the other holder is provably dead" rather than literally. That is candid and is
exactly the aliasing RFC §3 and the invariant-1 section sanction. Whether each invariant is
soundly upheld in depth is reviewer-safety's lens, not mine.

13. "REVIEW: fail_stop is the only place outside boot_rust that mints a device, and it cannot be used
for ordinary output" — SATISFIED (RFC C23 exactly). `grep -rn 'BootConsole::new|PowerControl::new'
kernel/src` gives two call sites each and no more: boot.rs:122/126 inside boot_rust, and fail.rs:31/35
inside fail_stop. It cannot be used for ordinary output: Failure is a unit struct that does not
implement hal::Console; fail_stop has no receiver, returns `!`, and its one caller (panic.rs:44)
passes the compile-time PANIC_MARKER constant. There is no accessor, no free function returning
authority, no print!/println! macro and no console.rs anywhere in the tree.

NON-GOALS. None appear. No VBAR_EL1 or vector table; no MMU, TTBR, TCR, MAIR, TLBI or page tables
(SCTLR_EL1 = 0x30d00800 leaves M, C, I, A, SA, SA0 clear); no GIC or interrupt handling (DAIF masked
at the first instruction and never unmasked); no device tree or FDT parsing and x0 is never read; no
PL011 initialisation (no LCR_H, IBRD, FBRD or CR write); no timers, CNTVOFF or CNTHCTL; no CPACR or
FP/SIMD; no core::fmt (nm reports no fmt symbol; the core::fmt strings in the file live only in the
unallocated .debug_str); no PanicInfo on the wire; no kernel/tests and no #[cfg(test)], so
ci/build.sh --test reports SKIP and not FAIL (RFC C3); no second architecture, no real-hardware
support, no performance work. The only textual hit for a non-goal construct in the whole tree is
"VBAR_EL2" inside a boot.rs comment explaining why the EL2 drop was removed.

SECONDARY-CORE PARKING — asked about explicitly, so answered explicitly. Its absence is CORRECT, not
a dropped requirement. The pinned RFC (8bbd8709...) lists "Secondary-core parking. No MPIDR_EL1
check." under Non-goals, with the reason: QEMU starts every non-primary CPU start-powered-off
whenever the PSCI conduit is enabled, so a park loop would be unreachable code in the privileged
image. It was present in an earlier revision of the design; the revision that governs here removed
it. Adding it would have been a non-goal violation and a blocking finding.

SILENTLY DROPPED REQUIREMENTS — none found. I diffed intent against every piece of near-complete code
the RFC gives. _start is instruction-for-instruction the RFC's sequence, in the RFC's order (DAIF
mask, .bss zero, __stack_top into x12, CurrentEL check, SCTLR_EL1 + isb, sp, branch, park at 4). main.rs,
hal.rs, panic.rs, arch/mod.rs, platform.rs, cpu.rs, fail.rs, link.ld and build.rs are the RFC's code.
pl011.rs fills in the bodies the RFC elided, per its prose: poll FR.TXFF, then write DR, per byte.
kernel/src/mem.rs was correctly not created (compiler_builtins supplied memcpy/memset as expected).
Two deviations, both recorded as findings below and neither a design change: psci.rs declares SMCCC
clobbers the RFC snippet omitted, and Cargo.toml adds `license` and a `[profile.dev]` section.

SCOPE. The implementation commit (7236c3d) touches exactly the fifteen files in task.scope.touches
and nothing else — no additions, no omissions. Nothing under does_not_touch is touched: ci/, rfcs/,
roadmap/, governance/, CONSTITUTION.md, constitution.toml and .provenance/ are untouched;
kernel/.cargo/ and kernel/kernel.ld do not exist on the branch (and never existed in any tracked
commit, so there was nothing to delete — the deliberate deletions the record mentions are absent from
the diff for that reason, not because they were skipped). The only path outside touches is the
tasks/open/ -> tasks/active/ rename of T-0002.toml, which is `forge claim`'s own commit (af28a38),
not implementation work.

COMMIT MESSAGE CLAIMS — all four reproduced.
- "E0277 from hal.rs when a trait impl and its only call site are removed": TRUE, reproduced verbatim
  (error[E0277] ... --> src/hal.rs:93:22).
- "__bss_start == __bss_end": TRUE. nm gives both as B 0x400800c0, and readelf shows .bss size 0.
  The claimed address 0x400800c0 matches.
- "191-byte image": TRUE. objcopy -O binary is 191 bytes, from both the committed target/ and a
  from-scratch rebuild, byte-identical.
- "no allocated PROGBITS after .bss": TRUE, per readelf -S above.
- Also verified: clippy clean under -D warnings; hal-boundary and no-kernel-deps pass; Cargo.lock
  resolves one package; QEMU exits 0 after PSCI SYSTEM_OFF. The message's own caveat about rust-lld
  is accurate and was disclosed rather than hidden, which is the right instinct.

VERDICT. Every one of the thirteen acceptance criteria is satisfied; four were judgement calls and I
tested three of them mechanically rather than reading them. No non-goal appears. The design is the
RFC's design, not a neighbouring one. Nothing was dropped. Approve, with one major and two minor
findings, none of which is against the code: the task digest in the contribution record does not
reproduce by its own convention, the branch is behind the main that carries the linker resolution,
and the manifest carries two keys the RFC's manifest does not.

findings.issue: `PowerControl::new` and `BootConsole::new` (pl011.rs:30) are `pub`, and `arch/mod.rs:19` re-exports both types crate-wide, so any module in the kernel can mint either authority. `PowerControl::new()` is nullary: no address, no argument, none of the six constructs the HAL check greps for. Verified — a portable module containing only `unsafe { crate::arch::PowerControl::new() }.off()` compiles clean and passes `ci/constitution-check.sh --check hal-boundary`. RFC-0001 calls the two-call-site rule 'mechanical, that rule is criterion C23', but C23 is listed under REVIEW and nothing runs it.
findings.why_it_matters: This is the RFC's central invariant-1 claim -- ownership does at M0 what a capability does at M4 -- and it rests on a review criterion the gate does not execute. Unforgeability here is relative to safe code only; the kernel is entirely privileged code and `unsafe` is available in every file (there is no `[lints]` section and clippy runs defaults, so `undocumented_unsafe_blocks` is off -- a reach-around needs no SAFETY comment to pass CI). Under invariant 2 this is the worse half: a nullary constructor is not merely a cached authority revocation cannot reach, it is one re-derivable from nothing by any holder, which is what makes 'revoke' unmeaningful. The RFC's own Alternatives section rejects the free-function HAL because 'two public free functions in arch/ ARE ambient authority -- the ability to write to the console and to power the machine off, reachable by position from every line of the kernel'; two `pub unsafe fn new` re-exported from `arch` are the same reach with an `unsafe` keyword in front. Fix, verified: `pub` -> `pub(super)` on both constructors. The kernel builds byte-for-byte unchanged (boot.rs and fail.rs are both inside `crate::arch::aarch64`), the conformance block in hal.rs is unaffected because it names only types, and the reach-around now fails with E0624 'associated function `new` is private'. Two words turn C23 from a criterion each future reviewer must re-derive from an RFC into a boundary the compiler enumerates. It stays cheap only until the first module between now and M4 uses the ambient path.

findings.issue: `task_sha256 = "06ede98398b95407176b421fc6d358593cd9f195f5e1fbc080e4f87464feda73"` does not match the task it pins. `sha256sum tasks/active/T-0002.toml` on the branch -- and `tasks/open/T-0002.toml` on main, byte-identical -- is `e2d48afbea31e83d73b4bc65fd174a5bd5d56fe3726f7ad0a6209315c9e29a15`. The recorded value is the digest of the same bytes with the trailing newline stripped, i.e. the pre-`e52de87` `forge` bug. The record is timestamped 16:16:29, the same second the fix commit landed. `rfc_sha256` is correct and I verified it: `8bbd8709...` matches rfcs/0001-aarch64-boot.md on main, in the worktree, and in the branch -- the C-0001 finding about the RFC pinned by bare identifier is genuinely fixed at the record level.
findings.why_it_matters: Invariant 3 is enforced now, and the gate checks well-formedness while this role checks truth. A 64-hex field that resolves to a different document than the one named is a false claim in the provenance record of what will be the ledger's first gate-passed line, and it is precisely the defect `e52de87` was written to prevent: 'provenance that needs archaeology to confirm is weaker than provenance that verifies on sight'. Here it does not verify at all -- an auditor running `sha256sum` gets a different number and has no way to know whether the task changed or the hasher was broken. I did not grade it blocking: `.forge/` is gitignored so the field never enters the repository, `ci/gate.sh` does not copy `task_sha256` into the ledger line, and traceability survives through `task = "T-0002"` and the file in the tree. But `evidence_digest` is computed over this directory at merge time, so merging as-is makes the ledger permanently attest to a record containing a false digest. Remedy: re-run `forge submit` with the fixed script, or correct the one field. No code changes, and no re-review of the patch is required.

findings.issue: `unsafe fn fail_stop(bytes: &[u8]) -> !` accepts arbitrary runtime bytes. Of the five bounds RFC-0001 places on this seam, three are compiler-enforced (never returns, not a `Console`, no receiver) and two are not: 'one caller' and 'emits one compile-time constant and cannot be asked to emit anything else'. Both reduce to the same review-only property, and the second is stated as if it followed from the signature. Verified: a portable module containing `unsafe { crate::arch::Failure::fail_stop(secret) }` for an arbitrary `&[u8]` compiles clean and passes the HAL check.
findings.why_it_matters: Asked directly whether the bounding is real or a global console with a narrow doorway: it is real, and narrower than a global console -- divergence means it can be used at most once per execution and nothing runs after it, so it can never become a channel for ongoing output, and the shipped image proves the point (the 191-byte artefact contains `SKYNET_BOOT_OK` and nothing else; `SKYNET_PANIC` and the whole fail_stop path were garbage-collected as unreachable). What it is, precisely, is a one-shot arbitrary-bytes emit-and-die primitive reachable from any kernel module without a token. That is a telemetry primitive of bandwidth 'one message, once, at death', and invariant 5 has no floor on bandwidth. Today invariant 5 is exactly true because the only caller passes a `const`; the signature does not make it true. Fix: `bytes: &'static [u8]`. At M0, with no allocator and no statics, `'static` means compile-time data, so the RFC's stated bound becomes a type-level property rather than a convention -- and when an allocator arrives the constraint is already written down where the next author will read it. hal.rs already lists 'being handed anything but a compile-time constant' as one of the four things that must never happen; one lifetime makes the compiler responsible for one of the four.

findings.issue: 'Portable code reaching for an architecture type would not type-check.' That is false as written. `kernel_main`'s own parameters are opaque -- which is the true and valuable half -- but `mod arch;` at crate root is visible crate-wide and `arch/mod.rs:19` re-exports `BootConsole`, `Failure`, `PowerControl`, `Processor`, so any portable module may `use crate::arch::BootConsole;` and it compiles. Verified for all four types.
findings.why_it_matters: A doc comment is part of the record, and this is the sentence a reader at M4 will cite as evidence that the question was settled -- which is exactly when nobody re-checks it. The types must stay crate-visible because hal.rs's conformance block names them, and naming a type grants nothing; the accurate statement is that portable code cannot *obtain* a device except by hand-over, which becomes true once the constructors are `pub(super)`. Reword to say what is enforced, or make it true, but do not leave the strong version standing on the weak fact.

reviewer_verdicts.reasoning:
Approve. No blocking finding. Two major, two minor, three notes. The blocking finding I raised against C-0001 is completely fixed, and I checked the fix by the standard the finding was made under rather than by the standard the script enforces.

WHAT I VERIFIED, AND HOW. I built, linted, size-checked, boot-tested and constitution-checked the branch in its worktree with the supplied toolchain, and I ran four separate probe crates against copies of the kernel to test structural claims that reading cannot settle. Everything below marked 'verified' I executed.

THE C-0001 BLOCKING FINDING IS CLOSED, COMPLETELY. `kernel/src/arch/aarch64/link.ld` exists, `build.rs:27` points at it through `CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR`, and `kernel/kernel.ld` is gone. I then did what the finding actually demands, which is to search for hardware addresses in every file type rather than in the six greps: across all sixteen files the contribution touches, the only hex literals of four digits or more are `0x0900_0000` (platform.rs), `0x8400_0008` (psci.rs), `0x30d0_0800` and `0x0800` (boot.rs), `0x000`/`0x018` (pl011.rs), and `0x40080000`/`0x10000` (link.ld) -- every one inside `kernel/src/arch/aarch64/`. `kernel/Cargo.toml`, `kernel/Cargo.lock` and `kernel/build.rs` contain none. The repository-root `.cargo/config.toml` added on main at `e1f0e77` contains none either; it sets one linker binary and names one target triple, which is finding-note 5's subject and not an address. The `tasks/active/T-0002.toml` hits are the task brief's own quotation of the C-0001 finding and of the QEMU memory map, in a file this contribution only renames (zero content change, authored by the decomposer on main) -- a specification document, not code. `ci/constitution-check.sh --check hal-boundary` passes. So does the C15 grep by hand.

INVARIANT 1, NO AMBIENT AUTHORITY (pending, M4). I was asked to interrogate the claim, so I did rather than reading the argument.

Zero statics: true, and I verified it three ways rather than by grep alone. `grep -rnE '\bstatic\b'` over kernel/src returns two hits, both inside a comment in boot.rs explaining why there are none. No `UnsafeCell`, `Cell`, `Atomic*`, `Once`, `thread_local`, `#[used]`, or `extern "C" {}` block anywhere. And decisively, in the linked image: `.bss` is a NOBITS section of size 0, `__bss_start == __bss_end == 0x400800c0`, so the claim is a property of the artefact and not of the source. The `.bss`-zeroing loop in the disassembly loads the same address into x10 and x11 and exits on its first comparison. The commit message's exact number is right.

Ownership doing a capability's work: the shape is correct and better than I expected. Both device types have private fields, both constructors are `unsafe`, `Power::off(self)` consumes, `kernel_main<C: Console, P: Power>` cannot name a concrete device in its signature, and the monomorphised code in the image is a fifteen-byte write loop followed by `hvc` with `#0x8400_0008` in w0 -- the abstraction costs nothing. `BootResources` is a two-field bundle handed once and never stored, which is the shape the RFC promises to keep.

Where it does not hold is visibility, and that is finding 1. `pub const unsafe fn new` on both constructors plus a crate-wide re-export means both authorities are reachable by position from every module in the kernel. `PowerControl::new()` takes no argument at all, so reaching it requires no address literal and none of the six checked constructs -- I compiled a portable module that powers the machine off and it passed both the build and the HAL check. The RFC calls its two-call-site rule 'mechanical'; it is not, it is criterion C23 under the REVIEW heading, and nothing runs it. `pub(super)` fixes it: I applied it to both constructors, the kernel built unchanged, and the reach-around then failed with E0624. Two words, and the difference between a rule enforced by whoever reads RFC-0001 and a rule enforced by rustc.

Does `fail_stop` bound authority or merely narrow the door to a global console? Real, and narrower than a global console, but two of its five bounds are not what the RFC implies. Compiler-enforced: it diverges, it has no receiver, `Failure` does not implement `Console`. Because it diverges it can be used at most once on any path and nothing runs afterwards, so it can never become a channel for ongoing output -- that is the load-bearing bound and it is genuine. Not compiler-enforced: 'one caller', and 'cannot be asked to emit anything else', which is the same property stated twice. `fail_stop(bytes: &[u8])` will accept anything; I compiled a portable module that pushes arbitrary runtime bytes through it. So what exists today is a one-shot arbitrary-bytes emit-and-die primitive reachable from any module without a token. What would make it a global console is written correctly in both hal.rs:55 and fail.rs:18 -- returning, gaining a receiver, gaining a second call site, being handed non-constant bytes -- and `&'static [u8]` would hand the fourth of those to the compiler for one word (finding 3). Whether the second bootstrap-mirror exemption is legitimate at all is a question the constitution cannot currently answer, which is note 6.

Can portable code reach `crate::arch::BootConsole` or `Failure` directly? Yes, all four re-exported types, verified. Naming a type grants nothing and the conformance block needs them nameable; it is the constructors that must narrow. `Failure::fail_stop` needs no constructor and no address at all.

Will this have to be rewritten at M4? No. The traits become what a capability wraps, `BootResources` becomes whatever mints the initial set, `Power::off(self)` is already right. The two things that will need work are the ones this review names: the constructors' visibility, and the eventual diagnostic path the RFC flags as O-4.

INVARIANT 2, USER SOVEREIGNTY (pending, M5). State the ledger would need: none exists. `.bss` is zero bytes, there is no allocator, no persistence, no interior mutability, no clock, no counter, and no value survives `boot_rust`'s frame -- `power` is consumed by `off()` and `console` is dropped at a divergence that never arrives. Cached authority revocation would not reach: none, in the ordinary sense. But finding 1 is the sharper form of the same failure. A nullary `pub unsafe fn new() -> PowerControl` is not a cached authority; it is one re-derivable from nothing by any holder, and an authority you cannot cache because you can always re-mint it is strictly worse for 'revoke' than one you can enumerate. That is the invariant-2 reading of the same two words. The first state that will actually need recording arrives when something holds a device token across a scheduling boundary, which is M2/M3, and I record here that at M0 there is nothing.

INVARIANT 5, ZERO TELEMETRY (pending, M6). Nothing can carry information outward, and I checked the artefact rather than the source. The 191-byte loadable image contains exactly one string: `SKYNET_BOOT_OK`. `SKYNET_PANIC` is not in it -- `.rodata` is fifteen bytes, and LTO plus `--gc-sections` removed the entire panic path as unreachable, which is the strongest possible confirmation that the failure path formats nothing. `PanicInfo` is discarded (`fn panic(_info: &core::panic::PanicInfo)`); no `core::fmt`, no `write!`, no `Debug`, no `Display`, no derive anywhere in the tree. The ELF carries no host path, no builder identity and no timestamp -- I grepped it for `/home`, `/tmp` and the user name and got zero hits. No error code varies with private state: every panic emits the same thirteen bytes and takes the same exit. The PL011 poll varies with FIFO occupancy, not with data; both marker writes are fixed-length, so there is no timing channel standing in for a data one. `overflow-checks = true` produces a marker and a shutdown, not a report. The one honest caveat is that `fail_stop`'s signature does not enforce what its caller currently does -- finding 3 -- and the boot console is genuinely an outward channel, correctly modelled as an owned resource rather than an ambient one so that it can be placed behind a capability at M6.

INVARIANT 6, SPIRIT. `hal.rs` is genuinely architecture-neutral: no `cfg`, no address, no register, no instruction, and -- checked specifically because it was a C-0001 finding -- no `usize`, no page-size assumption, no interrupt model, and no firmware-handoff parameter. The `_dtb` parameter is gone entirely; the portable entry point no longer has the shape of one firmware model. `Console::write` takes bytes, `Power::off` takes nothing, `Cpu::halt` takes nothing, `FailStop::fail_stop` takes bytes.

The conformance block makes the seam real rather than conventional, and I tested it rather than believing the commit message. I removed `impl Cpu for Processor` and its only call site (`Processor::halt()` in psci.rs), leaving `Processor` exported. The build fails with `error[E0277]: the trait bound 'Processor: Cpu' is not satisfied` pointing at `src/hal.rs:93`, with the required-by-bound note at `hal.rs:88`. C21, would main.rs, hal.rs and panic.rs compile unmodified against a second architecture: yes, and I proved it rather than reasoning about it. I deleted the entire `src/arch` tree, replaced it with a stub implementation in pure Rust with different device shapes and no aarch64 anywhere, and left the three portable files byte-identical (`diff -q` confirms). `cargo check` succeeds. The only failure in the full build is the linker script path, which is `build.rs` doing exactly its job for a target whose script I had deleted. The seam holds.

INVARIANT 10, ENGLISH. Pass, and this one is mine to judge. Every added line is English; the only non-ASCII codepoint in the entire diff is U+2014, the em dash, used as punctuation throughout. INVARIANTS 4, 8, 9. Budgets are the gate's and pass at 191 of 196608 bytes. Roadmap alignment is the Guardian's. Nothing here touches `roadmap/votes`.

PROMPT INJECTION. None. The comments argue their case at unusual length, but they argue to future implementers, not to me. `link.ld:8` states that a crate-root `kernel.ld` was a blocking finding on C-0001 and `boot.rs:62` states that reviewer-safety refused the EL2 drop; I checked both against the record rather than accepting them, and both are true. No file claims an exemption, asserts prior approval, or invokes authority it does not have. `arch/aarch64/mod.rs:8` volunteering that the linker script sits there 'even though the mechanical check cannot see it' is the opposite of an injection attempt.

WHY APPROVE. Every C-0001 finding I raised is addressed at the level it was raised: the linker script is inside the HAL and I confirmed the fix is exhaustive rather than local; `console.rs`, `print!`, `println!` and `_print` do not exist, and what replaced them is a `FailStop` trait with one caller, no receiver, no `Console` implementation and a divergent return -- a strictly smaller authority than the unit struct it replaces; the RFC is pinned by a content hash that matches; `PanicInfo` is discarded and the panic path is not even present in the shipped image; `_dtb` is gone from the portable seam. Of my four notes, one is fixed in the gate and three still stand and are re-filed here, one of them with the concrete instance it predicted.

What remains is two majors, neither of which meets this role's definition of blocking. The visibility finding does not make invariant 1 unachievable -- the fix is two words and the compiler enumerates every consequence -- but it does make it materially cheaper to fix now than after the first module between here and M4 uses the ambient path, which is the whole content of 'major'. The digest finding is a false field in a gitignored scratch record that the ledger does not carry; it must be corrected before the gate runs, and correcting it requires no re-review of a line of code.

FOR WHOEVER READS THIS AT M4. The three questions I would want answered about M0 are: were there globals (no -- verified in the artefact, `.bss` is zero bytes), was there a general console (no -- `SKYNET_PANIC` is not even in the image), and was device authority reachable without being handed over (yes, through `pub unsafe fn new` on two constructors and through `Failure::fail_stop`, and that is finding 1 and finding 3 in this record). If those two constructors are `pub(super)` by the time you read this, the RFC's invariant-1 argument is sound as written. If they are still `pub` and there are now more than two call sites, this is where that started.

findings.issue: The `hvc #0` asm declares only x0-x3 as clobbered; the SAFETY comment concedes SMCCC v1.0 permits x4-x17 corruption and dismisses it as "harmless here because the call is divergent - nothing after it reads a register", but the same function's next comment states the code below is "reached only if PSCI did not honour the call" and `Processor::halt()` follows the block.
findings.why_it_matters: The two comments argue opposite things about the same instruction, and the premise fails exactly on the firmware the fall-through exists for: one that returns NOT_SUPPORTED. On such a platform any value LLVM had allocated into x4-x17 across the block is silently destroyed. It is safe today only by codegen accident - I disassembled the linked image and the instructions after `hvc` are `msr daifset, #0xf; wfi; b .-4`, which touch no register - and by QEMU's SYSTEM_OFF never returning at all. `clobber_abi("C")` states the SMCCC v1.0 contract the comment itself invokes and costs nothing on a divergent call.

findings.issue: The failure path has no re-entrancy guard, and its SAFETY argument ("the kernel has already failed and this function never returns, so no other owner ... will run again") covers other owners but not `fail_stop` re-entering itself: a panic inside `Console::write`, `Power::off` or `Cpu::halt` re-enters the panic handler, which calls `fail_stop` again, without bound.
findings.why_it_matters: `overflow-checks = true` is enabled in release specifically so that arithmetic takes the panic path (Cargo.toml:29), which makes every future arithmetic operation on the failure path panic-capable by design. I reproduced the failure mode by adding one overflowing `u8` add to `BootConsole::write` and booting the result on the real target: the recursion overruns the 64 KiB `.stack`, which has no guard page because the MMU is off, and whose low end (0x400800c0) sits 192 bytes above `.text` at 0x40080000 - so it overwrites the kernel's own code, then takes an undefined-instruction exception to an uninitialised VBAR_EL1 (0) + 0x200, which is unmapped. 55.9 million exception entries in a 20-second run, zero console output, and CI sees only a 30-second timeout. Not blocking because the path is genuinely panic-free today: `write` does only a constant-offset `ptr::add` and a `u8 as u32` cast, the slice iterator is unchecked, `off` and `halt` have no arithmetic, and the shipped image contains no panic handler at all (`.text` is 0xb0 bytes: `_start`, `kernel_main`, `boot_rust`). Nothing enforces that it stays that way. A one-word re-entry flag, or moving the stack below `.text` so an overrun faults instead of corrupting code, would close it.

findings.issue: Two of the four SAFETY clauses do not hold as stated, and a fifth (alignment) is missing. (i) "The MMU is off ... so both accesses are to Device-nGnRnE memory" is not implied by SCTLR_EL1.M == 0 alone: stage-1-disabled data accesses at EL1 are Device-nGnRnE only when the Effective value of HCR_EL2.DC is 0 and stage 2 is disabled, and `_start`'s check establishes CurrentEL == 1, not the absence of EL2. (ii) "`&mut self` gives exclusive access ... the one aliasing exception is `Failure::fail_stop`" misidentifies the mechanism: `fail_stop` does not borrow this `BootConsole`, it constructs a second one over the same address, so no `&mut` rule is involved and `&mut self` never excluded that aliasing. (iii) The `*mut u8` -> `*const u32` / `*mut u32` casts need 4-byte alignment for `read_volatile`/`write_volatile` and the comment never says so.
findings.why_it_matters: The clauses are individually true on this target and I verified the parts that are checkable - `_start` parks on anything but EL1 (traced under `virt,virtualization=on` and `virt,secure=on`: both reach `0x40080054: wfi` and stay), FR at +0x18 is read-only with no read side effects and is only read, DR at +0x00 is read-write in the PL011 but is only written so the RX-FIFO pop side effect is never triggered, and 0x0900_0000 / 0x0900_0018 are both 4-aligned. But the arguments as written will not warn the next reader. The inference that actually closes clause (i) is that a *reset* entry observing CurrentEL == 1 proves EL1 is the highest implemented EL and therefore EL2 does not exist - a fact about `_start` being a reset vector, not about the EL check. Boot under a hypervisor at EL1 with HCR_EL2.DC == 1 and these same MMU-off accesses become Normal Cacheable: the poll of FR and the store to DR can sit in a cache line and the console silently stops working. What actually excludes the `fail_stop` aliasing is the two-call-site discipline (RFC-0001 C23), which is the clause worth writing down because it is the one a future edit can break.

findings.issue: `boot_rust`'s soundness rests on "Reached only from `_start`, exactly once" and "uniqueness is a property of the control flow, which has exactly one path here", but the reason a second core cannot take that same path is nowhere in this file.
findings.why_it_matters: The device tokens' "at most once" precondition is entirely load-bearing here, and the fact that upholds it - QEMU virt sets `start-powered-off` on every non-primary CPU whenever the PSCI conduit is enabled - lives only in RFC-0001 (lines 56 and 708-711), not next to the `unsafe` that depends on it. I confirmed the removal of the MPIDR park is sound as claimed: `-smp 2` and `-smp 4` each print SKYNET_BOOT_OK exactly once and exit 0. But `ci/boot-test.sh` never passes `-smp`, so the assumption is tested by nobody, and a configuration that reaches `_start` on several cores (EL3 firmware handing off at EL1, PSCI conduit disabled) would have every core mint its own `BootConsole` and `PowerControl` over the same devices. One sentence at the mint site, naming the platform fact, is what makes this checkable in five years.

findings.issue: The fall-through argument covers exactly one failure mode - "firmware that does not implement SYSTEM_OFF returns NOT_SUPPORTED" - and not the case the comment's own premise excludes: a conduit that is not HVC, or PSCI disabled, where `hvc #0` is UNDEFINED rather than returning.
findings.why_it_matters: In that case control does not reach `Processor::halt()` at all; it vectors to an uninitialised VBAR_EL1. I observed that behaviour directly while reproducing the panic-recursion finding: an endless exception loop at 0x200 with no console output. RFC-0001 records the absent vector table as a deliberate M0 omission (lines 701-707, 1039-1041), so this is an incomplete argument rather than an unwritten assumption - worth one clause because `options(noreturn)` was correctly rejected on the same reasoning.

findings.issue: `.bss` is zeroed before `CurrentEL` is read, so a non-EL1 entry performs up to `(__bss_end - __bss_start) / 8` stores before it parks.
findings.why_it_matters: Harmless today and harmless while the entry EL has the MMU off - and .bss is currently empty, so the loop executes zero times (`__bss_start == __bss_end == 0x400800c0` in the linked image, both 8-aligned). Recorded only because the check costs four instructions and reordering it would make the park unconditional. The loop itself is correct and its stated argument holds: the linker script's `ALIGN(8)` on the output section and the trailing `. = ALIGN(8)` make both bounds 8-aligned and the span a multiple of 8, so `str xzr, [x10], #8` with `b.hs` terminates exactly on `__bss_end` and cannot overrun.

findings.issue: `write` polls `FR.TXFF` (transmit FIFO not full) rather than `FR.BUSY` or `FR.TXFE`, so it returns once the device has accepted the last byte, not once it has transmitted it; `fail_stop` then issues SYSTEM_OFF immediately.
findings.why_it_matters: `hal::Console::write` documents "accepted", which is honest, and under QEMU nothing is lost because the PL011 model pushes to the chardev on the DR store - I verified SKYNET_PANIC arrives in full before the clean exit. On real hardware the tail of SKYNET_PANIC can be cut off by the power-down, in the one path whose entire purpose is to be visible. Worth writing down before the first board where it matters.

I verified the RFC pin first: rfcs/0001-aarch64-boot.md hashes to 8bbd8709...fd9b on the branch, on main and in the working tree, matching contribution.toml. Nothing in the diff, the commit message or the code comments attempted to direct my review; the commit's account of what it fixed is a claim I re-derived rather than accepted.

I built and booted this myself for aarch64-unknown-none-softfloat with the committed .cargo/config.toml linker and QEMU 10.2.2 virt: SKYNET_BOOT_OK, no panic, PSCI SYSTEM_OFF, exit 0. I then disassembled the 0xb0-byte .text and read the emitted instructions, which is where two of the findings come from.
