On the C-0001 blocking finding: the fix is real, not asserted. `_start` reads CurrentEL, compares against 1, and branches to a `wfi` park otherwise; there is no EL2 drop anywhere in the tree. I traced it rather than reading it - `-M virt,virtualization=on` (reset at EL2) and `-M virt,secure=on` (reset at EL3) both walk `msr daifset`, the empty .bss loop, `mrs x9, currentel`, `b.ne`, and stop at 0x40080054 `wfi`. EL0 is the one level the park does not cover, because `msr daifset` and `mrs CurrentEL` are both UNDEFINED at EL0 and trap on the first instruction - but reset always enters at the highest implemented EL, so EL0 entry is not reachable, and that same fact is what makes the EL1 check strong: observing CurrentEL == 1 at a reset vector proves EL1 is the highest implemented EL, hence no EL2 and no EL3. That inference is the real load-bearing one and it is the one the pl011 SAFETY comment does not make (finding 3).

My other C-0001 findings, each re-checked. (a) SCTLR_EL1 is now written and the value is right: 0x30d0_0800 sets bits 11, 20, 22, 23, 28 and 29 - exactly the ARMv8.0 RES1 set for SCTLR_EL1 including SPAN, each of which selects ARMv8.0 behaviour on later cores - with M, A, C, I, SA, SA0, EE and E0E clear, and bits [63:32] zeroed by the `movz`. The `isb` is present and correctly placed before `mov sp` and the branch into Rust. The write happens after the EL check, so it is never issued at EL2 or EL3. (b) The clobber claim now states v1.0's rule correctly, but its justification is contradicted four lines later - finding 1. (c) The MPIDR mask is gone because secondary-core parking was removed entirely; I confirmed the platform fact it relies on with `-smp 2` and `-smp 4` (marker once, exit 0), so the removal is sound, but the fact is documented only in the RFC and never exercised by CI - finding 4. (d) No longer a proxy: this is the real target, real linker script, real machine.

The two things I want a human reading this in five years to know. First, the failure path is the least-tested code in the kernel and the only code that is entirely absent from the shipped image - `--gc-sections` and LTO eliminate the panic handler because nothing currently panics, so it has never executed on any target. I built a copy with a forced panic and confirmed it does work end to end (SKYNET_BOOT_OK, SKYNET_PANIC, exit 0), and then built a copy where the panic occurs inside `Console::write` and watched it recurse off the end of a stack that has no guard and sits directly above the kernel's own code. That is finding 2, and `overflow-checks = true` is what makes it a live concern rather than a hypothetical. Second, the design's device aliasing is not controlled by the borrow checker: `fail_stop` mints a second `BootConsole` rather than borrowing the first, so `&mut self` is not what keeps the two apart and there is no Rust-level aliasing violation to find. What keeps them apart is a two-call-site rule enforced by a CI grep. That is a defensible choice, argued at length in the RFC, but the SAFETY comment attributes the guarantee to the wrong mechanism, and the wrong mechanism is the one a reader will assume still holds after the next change.

findings.issue: The exact sentence the RFC amendment identified as the load-bearing false claim -- "Portable code reaching for an architecture type would not type-check" -- is still in the kernel source, unchanged. I compiled a portable function that names crate::arch::PowerControl and calls .off() on the branch: it builds, and hal-boundary passes.
findings.why_it_matters: The repository now holds two versions of the same claim, the corrected one in the RFC and the uncorrected one in the file a reader opens first. For a contribution whose entire value is making claim and reality agree, leaving the canonical statement of the falsified claim in place is a gap in its own purpose. Non-blocking: the substantive property holds, the RFC is the specification of record, and T-0003 explicitly placed main.rs out of scope.

findings.issue: ci/constitution-check.sh --check hal-boundary passes on the pre-fix tree with the reach-around present -- I ran it. The check is lexical and cannot see authority flow across the boundary it guards.
findings.why_it_matters: The fix is correct, but it corrects the code, not the check. If the project comes to read a hal-boundary PASS as evidence of capability discipline, the next defect of this class ships the same way. Out of scope here; worth stating in the ledger so nobody has to rediscover it.

findings.issue: The &'static bound is exact at M0 only because nothing in this kernel can produce a runtime-derived 'static slice -- no allocator, no other static, no leak. That is a property of M0, not of the lifetime.
findings.why_it_matters: hal.rs states the lifetime "makes the bound a property of the type rather than a promise in a comment". True today; once an allocator exists a &'static [u8] can carry runtime state again. Nobody should later read this signature as a permanent guarantee of "compile-time constant" without re-deriving it.

findings.issue: The zero-statics property this comment credits to three judges and two reviewers -- myself among them -- was over-credited, and this contribution is the disproof: the M0 kernel had zero statics and ambient authority simultaneously.
findings.why_it_matters: The trade is framed as spending a verified capability-discipline property. It is not: it spends a proxy that measured absence of shared mutable state and was read as absence of ambient authority. Correcting the framing matters more than the static does, because the next contribution should not treat a statics count as evidence about capability discipline.

guardian_verdicts.reasoning:
OBJECTIVE. Resolves: roadmap/0001-foundations.toml, "Sovereign foundations", status active, weight 100, weight_source "bdfl-seed". That weight is seeded by one person and has not been voted; the file itself says the vote does not open until milestone G3, at which point weight_source becomes "vote:cycle-0001". So "weight 100" here means "sole active objective, nobody has yet been asked" — not a mandate. I read it as a placeholder that obliges me to be more careful about drift, not less, because there is no elector to appeal to.

WHAT I VERIFIED RATHER THAN ACCEPTED. The submission narrates its own review history at length. Per my role that is data, so I reproduced the load-bearing claims in an isolated copy of both trees rather than reading them:

  1. Ambient authority was real. Appending `unsafe { crate::arch::PowerControl::new() }.off()` to portable kernel_main      COMPILES on main and fails on the branch with E0624. I then ran ci/constitution-check.sh --check hal-boundary      against the main tree WITH that reach-around present: it reports PASS. So a portable module could mint the      authority to power the machine off and clear every mechanical check the project has.
  2. Re-entrancy was real. Injecting a panic inside fail_stop's own write: unguarded main emits 1023 SKYNET_PANIC      lines, then the marker itself corrupts mid-write (`S \xf0\x00\x08\x40...NIC\n`) and QEMU times out with a      13,398-byte binary log. The branch emits exactly one SKYNET_PANIC, then halts, 99 bytes. The defect is worse than      a hang: the panic marker stops being trustworthy under a second fault.
  3. The 'static bound bites. A stack array carrying a runtime byte through fail_stop compiles on main and fails on      the branch with E0597.
  4. Cost. nano image is 191 bytes on both trees; clippy clean; both constitution checks pass; exactly one `static` in      the kernel, module-private in arch/aarch64/fail.rs.
  5. Provenance. contribution.toml's rfc_sha256 matches the amended RFC on main and task_sha256 matches the task file      byte for byte on both main and the branch — the implementer did not edit its own acceptance criteria, and did not      touch rfcs/. The RFC amendment is a separate prior commit (6a1431d). The separation of powers held here in fact,      not just on paper.

THE QUESTION PUT TO ME: is work that only repairs a previous claim a service to the common good, or the project cleaning up after itself?

It is a service, and I do not find this close. The common_good names capability discipline FIRST and says a system granting ambient authority anywhere "cannot be made to stop later; every retrofit leaves a path". That warning is about a system that has run for years on ambient authority. What is in front of me is a 191-byte kernel, four source files, one caller, one merged commit, where the ambient path is removed before anything is built on it. Calling that a retrofit stretches the word past its purpose. If I rejected this, I would be saying the M0 kernel should keep a nullary public constructor for the power-off authority. That is plainly wrong, and the objective's own rationale_for_ordering asks for exactly this: a forge that "proves itself on real code within its first week". A forge that ships a defect, finds it by reading rather than by machine, and closes it in the next contribution IS the proof. The alternative history — where nobody read the claim — is the one that fails this objective.

What I will not soften: the claim WAS false for the whole of M0, and no mechanical check could see it (I confirmed that directly, finding 1 above). Capability discipline at M0 was a review-checklist item, not a language property. This contribution converts it. It does not un-ship the defect, and the ledger recording that is the provenance property working as designed rather than a blemish on it.

THE THREE PROPERTIES, SEPARATELY.

  Capability discipline — served strongly and directly. This is the substance. The fix draws the right line: portable   code can still be HANDED a PowerControl and call .off() on it (I compiled that on the branch; it builds), it simply   cannot MINT one. Use-what-you-were-given, cannot-forge is the capability model itself, four milestones before   invariant 1's test suite exists. Invariant 1 is `pending`, which per forge/prompts/README.md means it is enforced by   judgement — this is judgement doing that job.

  Provenance — served, and undervalued by the framing. The falsified claim was recorded as a correction attributing   the reviewer who found it, not silently edited away, and the trade was disclosed in the same breath as the benefit.   "Traceability reaches all the way down" is worth little if the root lines are flattering. These are not.

  Portability discipline — served only weakly, and I want this on the record. The HAL boundary is NOT stronger after   this change; I ran the check before and after and it passes identically, and it passed with the reach-around   present. What changed is that the thing the boundary was assumed to imply is now actually true. The check is   lexical and cannot see authority flow. Nothing here should fix that — it is out of scope — but if the project comes   to believe hal-boundary enforces capability discipline, the next defect of this class ships too. Recorded as a   finding.

THE TRADE, AND MY OWN PANEL'S PRIOR CLAIM. I was asked to say plainly whether a claim my panel previously endorsed was overstated. It was, and I was one of the judges who endorsed it.

"Zero statics" was offered as evidence that ownership was doing at M0 what a capability will do at M4. This contribution is the disproof: the M0 kernel had zero statics AND had ambient authority. A public nullary constructor made the power-off authority reachable from anywhere with no shared mutable state involved at all. Zero statics measured absence of shared mutable state and was read as absence of ambient authority; the reach-around shows those two came apart. The metric was not worthless — it was measuring the wrong thing, and my earlier verdict credited it for a property it did not establish.

That makes the trade easy rather than agonising, and I think the submission's own framing of it as a painful sacrifice is slightly self-flattering. The project is not spending a capability-discipline property; it is spending a proxy that this very contribution demonstrates was unreliable, while simultaneously buying the real property the proxy stood in for. Netted out, capability discipline at M0 is STRONGER after this contribution, not weaker. I checked IN_FAILURE against the objective's language myself rather than accepting the RFC's argument: no `pub`, unnameable outside its module, touched by one `swap` in one function, only reachable effect `Processor::halt()`. It confers nothing, attenuates nothing, and cannot be passed. It is not authority; it is a bit. Against that: a failure path that overwrites the kernel's own text and corrupts its own panic marker, reproduced. I would take this trade every time, and I would have taken it even if zero statics had meant what we said it meant.

NON-GOALS. Checked all six explicitly. No user space or EL0; no driver work (the pl011 change is a visibility keyword); no filesystem, network or persistence — an AtomicBool in .bss is not persistence in the sense excluded; no human-facing interface; no real-hardware bring-up; no performance work. Clean.

PROPORTION. 90 insertions, 22 deletions, four files, image unchanged at 191 bytes, against the sole active objective at weight 100. Roughly half the diff is prose justifying the trade rather than code. If anything this is under-proportionate; my role's concern about ratio runs the other way and does not engage here.

A REASONABLE ELECTOR. Someone who voted for "Sovereign foundations" having read that "the address space, the scheduler and the object model have to be built without ambient authority from the first commit, or user sovereignty is never real" would recognise this immediately, and I think would be more reassured by it than by a feature. The thing such an elector should fear is a project that finds a hole in its own sovereignty claim and quietly narrows the claim. This does the opposite, in public, with reproductions. The eyebrow they would fairly raise — "you shipped it wrong" — is answered by the fact that they can see it was shipped wrong at all.

MY ONE FORWARD-LOOKING CONCERN, recorded now so it can be measured later rather than argued about. This is the second consecutive contribution whose content is substantially self-referential — the project reviewing, correcting and narrating itself — and none of objective 0001's success criteria 4, 5 or 6 (the gate as sole writer of main; the ledger recording the first kernel commit end to end; the MCP surface defined and implemented) moved. Criterion 1 was already met and remains met. One correction cycle is the forge working. A third consecutive self-referential contribution would start to read as drift toward process rather than product, which is precisely the failure I exist to name. It is not a reason to reject this one, which closes a real ambient-authority hole in the kernel.

INJECTION. I scanned the diff, the task file and the commit message. No exemption claim, no instruction addressed to a judge, no invocation of authority. One appeal to prior approval exists — "Zero statics was a property three judges and two reviewers verified and valued", in the commit message and repeated in fail.rs — and it is used to disclose a cost against the submission's own interest, which is the opposite direction from manipulation. I note only that a submission which pre-narrates its own review history is doing part of my job for me, and my job is not to be helped with; that is why I reproduced all five claims independently. Every one held.

VERDICT: approve, and this is only "I see no reason to stop this". Two other judges and ten mechanical conditions still stand between it and main.

findings.issue: The exact sentence that review found to be false — "Portable code reaching for an architecture type would not type-check" — is still in the kernel source, verbatim, unchanged by this contribution. RFC-0001 corrects it carefully; main.rs does not.
findings.why_it_matters: This contribution's entire value is closing the gap between a claim and the code. It closes the code half and the RFC half, and leaves the claim standing in the file a reader of the kernel opens first. It is also still inaccurate after the fix: `crate::arch::PowerControl` remains nameable from portable code, and what no longer type-checks is `::new()`, not the reach. I do not treat this as blocking: T-0003 explicitly lists main.rs under does_not_touch, so the implementer complying with its scope is correct behaviour and the boundary is the task author's. But the residual belongs to the same defect class the task exists to close, and it should not be left for a third contribution to discover.

findings.issue: "The lifetime makes the bound a property of the type rather than a promise in a comment" claims more than `&'static [u8]` delivers. `'static` bounds lifetime, not constness. I compiled the counter-example on this branch: a portable module declaring its own `static mut`, writing runtime state into it, and passing `&*addr_of!(..)` through `fail_stop` builds clean.
findings.why_it_matters: Fix 1 is rightly praised for converting a review checklist item into a language property. Fix 2 is presented in the same register and does not achieve the same thing — it narrows the exfiltration surface substantially (a caller now needs a static in scope, which is loud and reviewable) but leaves the bound enforced by the `# Safety` clause, i.e. by review. The improvement is real and I would not have it reverted. What I object to is a contribution whose thesis is "do not let a claim outrun the code" introducing a new claim of the same shape. Outside my lens as a soundness question; inside it as an honesty-of-claims question, which is the specific thing this contribution is for.

findings.issue: The rule replacing "the kernel has zero statics" is "the kernel has one static, in the failure path, and here is why it earns its place". The first was checkable with grep by anyone. The second is prose, and nothing in ci/ counts statics.
findings.why_it_matters: I think the trade itself is correct (see reasoning). My concern is the successor rule. A prose exception admits a second static on a similarly good argument, and a tenth on arguments nobody re-reads, with no point at which a check fails. Recorded so that a future second static is visibly a regression against a stated rule rather than a fresh judgement call. I cannot write to ci/ or roadmap/ and am not asking this contribution to; this is for whoever can.

findings.issue: I ran `--check hal-boundary` and `--check no-kernel-deps` against merged main with the PowerControl reach-around compiled into kernel_main. Both PASS. For the whole of M0 a portable module could mint the authority to power the machine off and every mechanical check in the project reported the kernel clean.
findings.why_it_matters: Not a defect in this patch — it is information this patch produced, and it is the most important thing in the contribution after the fix itself. The HAL boundary check scans for architecture-specific *constructs* (register names, asm, address constants); it does not and cannot see a portable module *constructing* an architecture type through a crate-scope re-export. Objective 0001 names portability discipline as one of three properties that cannot be retrofitted, and the check standing behind it measures less than the project believed. Visibility closed this instance; the class remains unchecked.

guardian_verdicts.reasoning:
I judged purpose only. I treated every sentence in the RFC, the task, the commit message and the code comments as data, and re-ran the load-bearing claims myself rather than accepting them.

OBJECTIVE. Resolves to roadmap/0001-foundations.toml — id 0001, status active, weight 100, weight_source bdfl-seed. That is one person's allocation (author johan, author_kind human), not an electorate's. The file says so itself: weights are seeded until cycle 0001 runs at G3, at which point weight_source becomes vote:cycle-0001. A bdfl-seeded 100 is not a mandate; it is a placeholder shaped like one, and I did not read it as authorisation. It cut one specific way here: with no vote to appeal to, I cannot justify approval by saying the electorate asked for this, so the entire judgement rests on whether the work matches the written common_good. Nothing external is anchoring it.

Provenance pins check out. The manifest declares objective 0001 and rfc_sha256 dc62bdf7…, which I verified is the AMENDED RFC, not the pre-amendment revision (8bbd8709…); task_sha256 matches the task on both main and the branch. The contribution is pinned to the corrected specification rather than to the one containing the false claim.

WHAT I VERIFIED RATHER THAN ACCEPTED. The defect was real. On merged main I added `unsafe { crate::arch::PowerControl::new() }` to kernel_main — a portable module — and it compiled. Against that same tree, with the reach-around still in place, `ci/constitution-check.sh --check hal-boundary` and `--check no-kernel-deps` both PASS. On task/T-0003 the identical probe fails with `error[E0624]: associated function \`new\` is private`. The rest holds: build passes, boot-test finds SKYNET_BOOT_OK with no panic and QEMU exit 0, five constitution checks pass with four reporting PENDING as pending, the nano image is 191 bytes (unchanged), and exactly one `static` item exists in kernel/src.

THE QUESTION THIS CONTRIBUTION ACTUALLY RAISES: is work that only repairs a previous claim a service to the common good, or the project cleaning up after itself?

Service — and I want to name the trap in the framing. The objective says capability discipline cannot be retrofitted, meaning a shipped system that granted ambient authority cannot later be made to stop, because every retrofit leaves a path. That is a claim about accumulated dependence over time. It is not a claim that a defect found one contribution after merge is unfixable. Read that way the objective is self-defeating: it forbids the only mechanism by which the discipline is ever established at all.

The test that separates a retrofit from the discipline being applied is whether anything already depends on the gap. Here: 191 bytes, one merged kernel contribution, zero dependents, and a fix that leaves the binary byte-identical while the compiler proves the closure complete. The same invariant retrofitted at M4 would mean auditing a scheduler, an address space and an object model for surviving paths, and could never be proved complete. This is four tokens and an E0624. It is the discipline being applied at the earliest point at which anyone noticed, which is what "from the first commit" can actually mean in practice.

But I will not let "the system self-corrected" stand in for "the system was correct." The false claim was in the RFC, was reviewed, and was approved by three judges of whom I was one. I did not catch it. What caught it was a reviewer writing the code the claim said was impossible — the technique this whole apparatus depends on, and the one I failed to apply. That is a finding about the panel rather than about this patch, and my reasoning is the only place it can be recorded.

THE TRADE, AND WHERE I THINK MY OWN PANEL OVERSTATED. Asked plainly: yes, the claim my panel endorsed was overstated, and here is how. Zero statics was never the property that mattered. It was a proxy for "no ambient authority", and a poor one in both directions. A `static AtomicBool` that grants nothing, carries no information, cannot be read outside its module and cannot be reached outside the panic path is not ambient authority under any reading of invariant 1. Meanwhile the genuine ambient-authority defect — a nullary, crate-visible constructor for the power-off capability — sat in the same kernel, in the same review cycle, while the proxy was being verified and praised. The panel measured the stand-in and missed the thing it stood for. Spending the proxy to close a live defect that overwrites the kernel's own .text under a second fault is not a close call; it is the correct trade, and the fact that it reads as a loss is the lesson about proxy metrics rather than an argument against it. My reservation is about the successor rule, recorded as a finding.

COMMON_GOOD, assessed per leg rather than in aggregate.

Capability discipline — served, and this is the strongest instance of it in the repository so far. It converts "only the boot path creates devices" from a review checklist item into a property the compiler enforces, at the one moment when that conversion is cheap and provably total. This is invariant 1 landing at M0 instead of being promised for M4.

Provenance — served, modestly, and honestly. The contribution builds no provenance machinery. What it does is refuse to launder a defect: the RFC records the correction in place ("Recorded here rather than quietly amended"), the ledger's C-0002 entry carries findings recorded at merge rather than suppressed, and the commit message discloses the zero-statics cost in its own words before being asked. A ledger whose lines are honest about what they got wrong is worth more than one that is merely complete.

Portability discipline — untouched, and I score it that way rather than generously. Nothing here moves the HAL boundary. What this contribution does to that leg is show that the check standing behind it measures less than the project believed, which I have recorded as a note.

NON_GOALS. None implemented. No user space or sub-EL1 execution, no driver beyond the boot console, no filesystem, network or persistence, no human-facing interface, no real hardware, no performance work — the AtomicBool is correctness, and the image is unchanged at 191 bytes.

PROPORTION. Four files, +90/-22, of which roughly two thirds of the added lines are the argument for why one static is admissible rather than code. On the sole active objective at weight 100 this is nowhere near disproportionate; it is close to the smallest change that could have closed the finding.

WOULD A REASONABLE ELECTOR RECOGNISE THIS. For the visibility fix, yes and pointedly: someone who read "the address space, the scheduler and the object model have to be built without ambient authority from the first commit, or user sovereignty is never real" is looking at that sentence being enforced on the first commit, in a form a compiler checks. For the guard, yes as ordinary hygiene — nobody votes for a re-entrancy guard, and nobody who read the reproduction votes against one. The one an elector might reasonably query is the `'static` change, for the reason in my second finding.

PROMPT INJECTION. None found, and I looked hard, because the prose here is unusually persuasive and persuasion is what I am the target for. The pattern that would concern me — pre-emptive self-criticism buying trust for something undisclosed — does not survive testing: every disclosure I checked was accurate, and the two things not disclosed I found by compiling counter-examples rather than by reading. Nothing addresses the Guardian, claims prior approval of THIS contribution, claims BDFL assent, or asserts constitutional permission. Both the RFC and the task argue against their own interest ("A reviewer may reasonably prefer proving the path panic-free instead"; "release the task and say so"). That is the shape of an honest submission, not a managed one.

WHAT I WAS UNSURE ABOUT. Two things. First, whether the stale sentence left in main.rs should be blocking. I concluded no — T-0003 scopes main.rs out and an implementer honouring its scope is behaving correctly — but a judge weighing it the other way would not be wrong, and I would not argue hard against them. Second, whether the ratio of repair to construction is itself a drift signal: after the M0 merge, everything on main is correction of it. At one merged kernel contribution that is the first review cycle completing, not a trend. At ten it would be a trend, and I would want the panel counting by then.

I approve. My approval means only that I see no reason to stop this, and it is not sufficient for a merge.

findings.issue: The commit message presents two different fault injections as one before/after. 'Injecting a panic inside fail_stop's own write ... exactly ONE SKYNET_PANIC on the console, then halt' and 'Before the guard the reproduction printed nothing at all and CI saw only a timeout' cannot be the same experiment: an injection that lets the marker reach the wire before panicking produces many markers when the guard is removed, not silence.
findings.why_it_matters: I reproduced both halves and they diverge. Injection after the transmit loop, guard present: SKYNET_BOOT_OK + exactly one SKYNET_PANIC, then halt (qemu rc=124, 99-byte log). Same injection, guard neutralised: ~800 SKYNET_PANIC lines, then console garbage, then timeout — the stack running into .text. The RFC's own injection (overflow before any byte transmits), guard present: empty console, timeout — i.e. for the reproduction the RFC actually describes, the guard changes a stack-smash into a clean halt but leaves CI seeing exactly what it saw before, nothing and a 30-second timeout. Every individual sentence in the commit message is true; the contrast it implies was not demonstrated, and a reader takes away that the guard made the failure legible when it only made it bounded.

findings.issue: main.rs still asserts 'Portable code reaching for an architecture type would not type-check' — verbatim the claim RFC-0001 section 2 was amended to record as false, and the claim this whole task exists to repair. It remains false after the patch: hal.rs's own const-assertion block names crate::arch::PowerControl from portable code and type-checks. What now fails is E0624 on the constructor's privacy, which is not a type-check failure.
findings.why_it_matters: main.rs is under task.scope.does_not_touch, whose instruction is 'should need no change; if one does, say why in the submission rather than changing it quietly'. The implementer correctly did not edit it, but the submission does not mention it either, so the false claim survives unflagged in portable code while the RFC that corrects it sits one directory away. The next reader of main.rs learns the wrong invariant from the file the invariant is about.

findings.issue: The image is unchanged at 191 bytes because the entire failure path is absent from the linked artefact, not because the guard is cheap. readelf -S shows .bss with size 0 (__bss_start == __bss_end == 0x400800c0); nm shows only _start, kernel_main and boot_rust — no Failure, no fail_stop, no panic handler, no IN_FAILURE. lto = true plus --gc-sections strips the whole panic path because nothing reachable in M0 can panic. objcopy -O binary of main and of task/T-0003 are byte-identical.
findings.why_it_matters: The task's constitutional note predicts 'the guard costs one byte of .bss'; it costs zero, and for a different reason than a reviewer checking only the number would conclude. The shipped M0 image contains no guard at all — it materialises only when a reachable panic exists. That is why criterion 9 is undemonstrable without an injected panic, and why an unexplained '191 bytes, unchanged' should not be read as evidence that the guard is present and free.

findings.issue: RFC-0001 as pinned contradicts itself on statics. The amendment at lines 539-565 requires exactly one static, but four passages were not updated with it: line 603 ('Four lines, no static, no accessor, no formatting'), lines 869-870 ('No static or static mut anywhere in kernel/src, including arch/ ... the count is zero'), line 922 ('there is still no static'), and mechanical conformance criterion C9 at lines 1008-1009 ('no static item of any kind exists in the kernel'). The section 4 fail.rs code block at lines 586-603 is stale in the same way: it still shows fail_stop(bytes: &[u8]) with no guard.
findings.why_it_matters: C9 as written now fails against the very result the same RFC mandates. Nothing in ci/ greps for statics, so the gate is unaffected today, but an auditor running the RFC's own checkable criteria against the merged kernel gets a false violation on the single most contested property of this contribution. The implementer had to decide which half of the RFC to follow; they picked the right half, and should not have had to pick.

findings.issue: &'static [u8] is necessary but not sufficient for the prose bound it replaces. It forbids a stack slice, which is the leak review actually found, but a future static buffer or interior-mutable static would satisfy 'static while carrying runtime state to the wire.
findings.why_it_matters: Not a patch defect — this is precisely what RFC-0001 specifies, and it is a real strengthening over &[u8]. Recorded so the next revision does not read 'the lifetime makes the bound a property of the type' as meaning the type now enforces 'compile-time constant'. If that is the property wanted, it needs a const generic or a private newtype minted only from a const, and that is an RFC question rather than a review comment.

reviewer_verdicts.reasoning:
PINS. Both reproduce: rfc_sha256 matches rfcs/0001-aarch64-boot.md as amended, task_sha256 matches git show task/T-0003:tasks/active/T-0003.toml. Verified before reading anything else.

ENVIRONMENT. rustc/cargo 1.97.1, ld.lld from the scratch sysroot, qemu-system-aarch64 10.2.2. kernel/target deleted before every measurement, so nothing below is a cached result. All twelve criteria walked one at a time.

C1 ci/build.sh exits 0 — SATISFIED. Clean rebuild, 'PASS kernel built: skynet-kernel', exit 0.

C2 --lint zero clippy warnings — SATISFIED. 'PASS clippy clean' under -D warnings.

C3 boot test — SATISFIED. All three: SKYNET_BOOT_OK present, no panic, QEMU exited 0.

C4 nano size within 192 KiB — SATISFIED. 191 bytes against 196608.

C5 hal-boundary — SATISFIED. PASS.

C6 no-kernel-deps — SATISFIED. PASS.

C7 PROOF, reach-around must fail with E0624 — SATISFIED, REPRODUCED BY ME, not accepted on assertion. In a scratch copy of the worktree I added `unsafe { crate::arch::PowerControl::new() }.off();` to kernel_main. Result: `error[E0624]: associated function `new` is private`, pointing at psci.rs:34 `pub(super) const unsafe fn new()`. I then did the same for the console: `crate::arch::BootConsole::new(0x0900_0000)` gives the identical E0624 against pl011.rs:36, so both constructors are closed, not just the one the task names. I also built the identical reach-around against main: it compiles, exit 0. The defect was real, and this patch is what closes it.

C8 PROOF, non-static slice must fail to compile — SATISFIED, REPRODUCED BY ME. I put a stack-local `let runtime: [u8; 13]` in the panic handler and passed `&runtime` to fail_stop. Result: `error[E0597]: `runtime` does not live long enough ... argument requires that `runtime` is borrowed for `'static``. Exactly the error the commit message claims. The same probe against main compiles, exit 0.

C9 PROOF, the guard is reached and halts rather than recursing — SATISFIED, REPRODUCED BY ME, in both directions. Injection: a runtime-valued `acc += b` accumulator over `bytes` placed after the transmit loop in BootConsole::write, so overflow-checks fires only once every byte is on the wire. Guard present: console shows SKYNET_BOOT_OK then exactly one SKYNET_PANIC, then nothing — qemu killed at the 20s timeout, i.e. the kernel is parked in Processor::halt, 99 bytes of log, one marker. Guard neutralised (`if false && IN_FAILURE.swap(...)`, everything else identical): ~800 SKYNET_PANIC lines followed by console garbage and a timeout — the 64 KiB stack running into .text exactly as RFC-0001 describes. The guard is what produces the halt. I additionally ran the RFC's own injection (overflow before any byte transmits) with the guard present: empty console, timeout. That is the basis of the first finding.

C10 exactly one static, documented as the single exception with the argument — SATISFIED. `grep -rnE '^\s*(pub(\([^)]*\))?\s+)?static\s' kernel/src kernel/build.rs` returns exactly one item, fail.rs:40 `static IN_FAILURE: AtomicBool`. No static mut anywhere (the two grep hits are prose in boot.rs and fail.rs). On the documentation bar: the doc comment opens 'The kernel's only `static`', carries a '# Why it exists' section reproducing the recursion defect and its concrete failure mode, and a '# What it costs' section that states the zero-statics property being spent, names who verified it, and gives the argument for why this one earns its place — grants no authority, only reachable effect is halt instead of recurse, carries no information, unreadable outside the module, unreachable outside the panic path. I checked those four claims against the code and all four hold: the static is private to fail.rs and its only reader/writer is fail_stop, whose only caller is the panic handler. This is the RFC's own argument transcribed into the source rather than gestured at, which is what the criterion asks for.

C11 REVIEW, every unsafe carries a SAFETY comment upheld on every path — SATISFIED. Eleven unsafe sites: hal.rs:71 (# Safety on the trait method), pl011.rs:36 (# Safety) and :70 (SAFETY), panic.rs:44 (SAFETY), fail.rs:56 (impl of a trait method whose # Safety is on the declaration, as on main), :75 and :79 (SAFETY), psci.rs:34 (# Safety) and :60 (SAFETY), cpu.rs:19 and :29 (SAFETY), boot.rs:33 and :118 (# Safety), :122 and :126 (SAFETY). No regression, and the one SAFETY comment this patch rewrites is strengthened rather than weakened: fail.rs:69-74 now closes the gap it previously left open, 'the "at most once" clause ... the guard above makes it true of this function too', which is exactly what the guard buys and is true on every path since the second entry halts before the mint.

C12 REVIEW, the psci SMCCC comment no longer contradicts itself — SATISFIED. The old text justified declaring only x0-x3 by 'the call is divergent — nothing after it reads a register', four lines above a Processor::halt() fall-through that exists precisely because the call may return. The new text (psci.rs:47-59) states the ground as 'nothing is live across this call on either path' and explicitly disclaims the divergence argument. It matches the RFC's amended wording near-verbatim. Whether the liveness claim is sound is reviewer-safety's lens, not mine; the criterion asks only that the comment stop contradicting itself, and it does.

RFC CONFORMANCE, ELEMENT BY ELEMENT. The guard's shape is the RFC's shape with nothing added or reinterpreted: same item name IN_FAILURE, same AtomicBool, same false initialiser, same `swap(true, Ordering::Relaxed)`, same Processor::halt() on second entry, same rule that a second entry must not touch the console. The pub(super) change is on both constructors with the RFC's two rationales attached to the right ones (the 'more sharply here, this constructor takes no arguments' argument on PowerControl). The &'static bound is on the trait declaration in hal.rs, so it binds every implementation rather than one. The RFC's claim that pub(super) leaves the kernel byte-identical is not merely plausible, it is true: objcopy -O binary of main and of task/T-0003 compare byte-identical at 191 bytes. Nothing from the RFC's non-goals appears — no device tree, no vector table, no SMP, no MMU, no core::fmt, no print! macro, no accessor.

SCOPE. Exactly the four files task.scope.touches names, plus the tasks/open -> tasks/active rename that is the forge's standard claim step and has an identical precedent in C-0002's 'T-0002: claimed'. Nothing under does_not_touch: ci/, rfcs/, roadmap/, governance/, CONSTITUTION.md, constitution.toml and .provenance/ are unmodified, and main.rs, panic.rs, boot.rs and arch/mod.rs are untouched as the commit message states. No unscoped work.

RATIONALE CLAIMS. All three headline claims are true and I reproduced each rather than reading them: E0624 for the reach-around, E0597 for the non-static slice, one SKYNET_PANIC then halt for the guard. 'Unchanged: boot, marker, clean PSCI shutdown, 191-byte image, clippy clean, both constitution checks' is true. 'main.rs, panic.rs, boot.rs and arch/mod.rs are untouched' is true. The one place the rationale overreaches is the before/after framing of proof 3, filed as a minor finding; and the 191-byte invariance has an explanation the submission does not give, filed as a note.

VERDICT. Approve. Twelve criteria satisfied, three of them by counter-examples I compiled and booted myself in a scratch copy, with the worktree left clean and untouched. The patch implements the RFC's amended design element for element, and its two demonstrable effects — a reach-around that used to compile and no longer does, and a recursion that used to smash the kernel's text and now halts — are both verified against main as a control. No blocking findings. The two minor findings are about what the submission says rather than what it does, and the three notes are for the architect: an RFC that still tells a reader in four places that the kernel has no statics, a size number whose stability means something other than what it looks like, and a lifetime bound that is a real improvement but not the property its prose claims.

findings.issue: The fix closes the constructor route to device authority and leaves the identical route through the trait open: `unsafe { crate::arch::Failure::fail_stop(b"...") }` compiles from any portable module (verified, exit 0), minting a BootConsole and a PowerControl, writing caller-chosen bytes to the operator's console and powering the machine off.
findings.why_it_matters: These are the same two authorities the pub(super) change was filed against, still reachable by position rather than by hand-off, and the file's own claim that IN_FAILURE "cannot be reached outside the panic path" is false by the same route. The RFC's bound -- "one function, one caller" -- is exactly the kind of prose promise this contribution's rationale says is not good enough. A language-level closure is cheap and I compiled it: a zero-sized `PanicToken` with a private field constructed only inside panic.rs, threaded through FailStop::fail_stop -- the kernel builds unchanged and the reach-around becomes error[E0603]. Until then the reach-around survives the task that existed to remove it.

findings.issue: The RFC amendment that introduces IN_FAILURE landed in section 4 only. Conformance criterion C9 still requires "no `static` item of any kind exists in the kernel", and the invariant-1 section (lines 869-872) still asserts "No `static` or `static mut` anywhere in `kernel/src`" and "no atomic 'already taken' flag" -- both now false of the merged tree.
findings.why_it_matters: C20 names C9 as the mechanical approximation of invariant 1 at M0, and invariant 1 has no other check until M4. After this merges, the only standing rule about statics is one the tree violates, and nothing replaces it with "exactly one, at this path". A criterion that is already violated is a criterion nobody can apply to the second static -- which is how the project's own O-6 describes a check passing for the wrong reason. One line fixes it: C9 becomes "exactly one `static` in kernel/src, and it is IN_FAILURE in arch/aarch64/fail.rs". Not the implementer's to write -- rfcs/ is outside the role -- but it must not merge unnoticed.

findings.issue: The doc comment still reads "Portable code reaching for an architecture type would not type-check." The RFC corrected that claim after review (section 2, "Correction, after review"); the code was not corrected, and the submission says only that main.rs is "untouched" without noting that it still carries the falsified sentence.
findings.why_it_matters: This is the exact claim that caused T-0003 to exist, and it is still false -- now in a stronger form than when it was filed. Verified: `crate::arch::Processor::halt()` compiles from kernel_main with no `unsafe` at all, and `crate::arch::Failure::fail_stop(...)` compiles with one. T-0003's scope told the implementer to say why in the submission if main.rs needed a change; it needed one and nothing was said. The sentence sits in the file a reader treats as the kernel's summary of itself, so the false claim outlives the review that found it.

findings.issue: "The lifetime makes the bound a property of the type rather than a promise in a comment" (and fail.rs:52, "The `'static` bound on its argument now enforces the last of those") overstates what `'static` does. `'static` means lives-forever, not known-at-compile-time.
findings.why_it_matters: Verified by compiling: a `static mut` buffer written at runtime and passed as `&*(&raw const BUF)`, and `core::slice::from_raw_parts(runtime_addr, n)`, both yield `&'static [u8]` and both compile. The stack-array probe is genuinely closed (E0597) but the exfiltration class is not, and this same patch legitimises statics in the failure path -- so the O-4 diagnostics buffer (`static mut BUF` + `fail_stop(&BUF)`) is one edit away with nothing in the type system or in CI against it. Invariant 5 is being carried by a comment that says it is not being carried by a comment.

findings.issue: The central question, answered on measurement rather than argument: the static earns its place at M0. The branch image is byte-identical to main's (191 bytes), `.bss` is 0 bytes, and `nm` finds no fail_stop, no IN_FAILURE and no SKYNET_PANIC in the artefact -- the whole failure path is garbage-collected because the compiler proves nothing panics.
findings.why_it_matters: It grants no authority; it carries no information (reaching it from portable code is error[E0603]: module `aarch64` is private -- verified); it costs nothing in the shipped image; and the defect it prevents is real -- I removed the guard, re-ran the injection, and got unbounded re-entry (hundreds of SKYNET_PANIC lines, then timeout). It does not make invariant 1 harder at M4: it is private, one bit, one writer, no reader outside its module, and a capability system has nothing to wrap. Recorded in full because someone at M4 will ask why the zero-statics property was spent, and the answer is that it was spent on a live crash and cost zero bytes.

findings.issue: "One static in the failure path" is a stable boundary only as prose. Asked what the second static would be, the RFC's own open questions name three candidates: O-4's diagnostics buffer, O-7's bound on the UART spin (which needs a notion of time), and M2's per-CPU state.
findings.why_it_matters: Device-minting was given a rule with teeth -- C23, "a third call site is a design failure requiring an RFC". Statics were given no equivalent, and the criterion that would have carried one (C9) was left asserting the old, now-false rule. So the mechanism that stops the second static is a paragraph in an RFC that already contradicts itself about the first. This is the ratchet, and it is closable today by replacing C9 rather than by argument.

findings.issue: The alternative -- proving the path panic-free -- was dismissed as an argument that "needs to show the property holds for every future edit, not for today's code". At M0 it is not a prose obligation: it is a mechanical property of every build, and I measured it (.bss empty, PANIC_MARKER absent from .rodata, panic path gc'd from .text).
findings.why_it_matters: A build assertion of that property would hold for every future edit by construction, because it re-runs on every build -- so the RFC weighed only the human form of the alternative and not the machine form. It is still a defensible trade: such a check has a known expiry, failing the moment M1 adds the first fallible code, which is exactly when the guard is needed, and adding the guard early beats retrofitting it under pressure. Recorded so M4 can see both halves were on the table and which was chosen.

findings.issue: The guard does not restore legibility in the scenario the doc comment uses to motivate it. Reproduced with the guard present and the RFC's own injection (an overflowing addition in the console write path): the console produces zero bytes and CI sees only a timeout -- the same symptom the comment attributes to the guard's absence.
findings.why_it_matters: What the guard actually buys is that the kernel stops instead of running its 64 KiB stack into `.text`; it does not buy a readable log. The doc's symptom list conflates the two, and the commit message's "Before the guard the reproduction printed nothing at all and CI saw only a timeout" invites the reader to think that half is solved. It is not, and O-4/O-7 still own it.

findings.issue: Standing note from C-0002, re-checked and still standing: the bootstrap exemption RFC-0001's invariant-1 argument leans on twice exists only in forge/prompts/reviewer-constitution.md. `grep -rn bootstrap CONSTITUTION.md constitution.toml governance/` returns nothing.
findings.why_it_matters: An exemption to an entrenched invariant that lives in a role prompt is amendable by whoever edits the prompt, outside the amendment procedure that invariant 1 is entrenched behind. It is now load-bearing for a second decision -- the RFC argues fail_stop is admissible as "the mirror image of the bootstrap exemption" -- so each design that leans on it makes the missing text more expensive to add. Either the constitution states the exemption and its limits, or the exemption stops being cited as authority.

findings.issue: Standing note from C-0002, re-checked and materially weaker but not gone: the repo-root .cargo/config.toml names aarch64-unknown-none-softfloat and selects the linker, so three committed places bind the build to an architecture while arch/mod.rs and the RFC both say two, and C10's grep covers only kernel/src and kernel/build.rs. The file is now thoroughly self-documenting, which is most of what was asked.
findings.why_it_matters: What remains untrue is the record, not the tree: RFC-0001's O-1 is still headed "(blocking, environment)" and lists its option 3 as unenacted, though option 3 is what landed in commit e1f0e77 and closed it. Invariant 3 is enforced now and asks the record to be true, not merely well-formed; a design document that reports a blocking question open after it was closed misleads the next reader about what the build depends on.

findings.issue: Standing note from C-0002, re-checked and unchanged: invariant 6's check greps kernel/src for six constructs. It does not read kernel/src/arch/aarch64/link.ld, kernel/build.rs, or .cargo/config.toml.
findings.why_it_matters: The invariant says "not one address constant" outside the HAL directory; the linker script is full of them and is invisible to the check, as the RFC itself observes. The letter is narrower than the meaning, which is the exact class of gap O-6 already found twice in this same script. Not touched by this patch; re-verified so the note does not lapse by silence.

reviewer_verdicts.reasoning:
I verified the three proofs the submission claims were RUN, independently, in a scratch copy -- all three are true, not merely well-formed. (1) `unsafe { crate::arch::PowerControl::new() }.off()` in kernel_main now fails with error[E0624]: associated function `new` is private; so does BootConsole::new. pub(super) from inside arch/aarch64/* does stop at arch::aarch64, and re-exporting the type through arch/mod.rs does not widen the associated function -- the fix is sound in the direction it points. (2) A stack array passed to fail_stop fails with error[E0597]. (3) Injecting a panic inside fail_stop's own write after a first panic yields exactly ONE SKYNET_PANIC and then halts; removing the guard and re-running the same injection yields unbounded re-entry, hundreds of markers, then timeout. The counterfactual is real and the guard demonstrably closes it. Mechanically: build, clippy, boot (marker present, no panic, QEMU exit 0), both size budgets, hal-boundary and no-kernel-deps all pass; the image is byte-identical to main's at 191 bytes; the tree contains exactly one static; nothing outside the four permitted files and the task rename is touched; everything is in English.

On the central question -- whether the kernel's first static is worth the zero-statics property -- I judge yes, and on measurement rather than on the RFC's argument. The static is private (reaching it from portable code is E0603), holds one bit, has one writer and no reader outside its module, grants nothing, and is currently absent from the artefact altogether: .bss is zero bytes and nm finds no fail_stop, no IN_FAILURE and no SKYNET_PANIC, because the compiler proves the M0 kernel cannot panic and --gc-sections removes the whole path. It will not have to be rewritten at M4; a capability system has nothing here to wrap. Against that stands a live defect with a reproduction. That trade is correct.

What I do not accept is that the boundary around it is stable. The RFC gave device-minting a rule with teeth (C23) and gave statics none, and the criterion that carried the old rule (C9, which C20 names as invariant 1's only mechanical approximation before M4) was left asserting zero statics -- false the moment this merges, and unreplaced. The second static is already named in the RFC's own open questions, and this same patch removes the other barrier to the most likely one: `'static` does not mean compile-time constant, so `static mut BUF` plus `fail_stop(&BUF)` compiles today. I verified that, and the from_raw_parts variant.

The reason this is approve and not reject: the contribution does what T-0003 asked, its headline claims are true, it closes a real authority hole and a real crash, and it costs nothing. The reason it carries three majors: the hole it closed has a sibling that is still open and is closable in six lines -- I compiled a PanicToken variant that turns the fail_stop reach-around into E0603 -- and the false claim in main.rs that caused this task to exist was left standing and unmentioned. A contribution whose purpose is "the claim was false, make it true" should not merge adding three new claims stronger than what the code enforces. None of that violates an enforced invariant or makes a pending one unachievable, so none of it is blocking; all of it gets more expensive after M1.

For whoever reads this at M4: the shape of M0 is right. Devices are values with private fields, created at named call sites, moved not fetched; there is no accessor, no registry, no print! macro, and now no crate-visible constructor. The one thing that is not yet a property of the language is the failure path's caller, and it can be made one before the second architecture makes it thirty files instead of three.

findings.issue: "`&'static [u8]`, not `&[u8]` ... The lifetime makes the bound a property of the type rather than a promise in a comment" is not true. `'static` excludes a borrow of a stack local; it does not exclude runtime state. A `static mut` buffer mutated at runtime, or `core::slice::from_raw_parts(p, n)` over arbitrary kernel memory (whose lifetime is inferred and unifies with `'static`), both satisfy the bound and neither needs anything the old signature did not already need.
findings.why_it_matters: I did not argue this, I booted it: `static mut SECRET: [u8;14]` with byte 12 written at runtime, passed as `&'static [u8]`, prints `leaked-nothiG` on the PL011 — the `G` is the runtime write. A second form needs no static at all: `from_raw_parts(sp as *const u8, 8)` reads the stack pointer with `mov {}, sp` and compiles clean, which puts arbitrary kernel stack on the operator's console through the one path whose entire purpose is to carry no private state. The E0597 probe the implementer ran is genuine and I reproduced it, but it demonstrates only the stack-local case. The invariant the patch says is now enforced by the type — "writes a compile-time constant and nothing else" — is still enforced exactly as it was before: by there being one call site, checked by review. The change is a real narrowing and worth keeping; the sentence claiming it is a type-level guarantee is what a future reader will rely on and it will not hold.

findings.issue: "Visibility is what makes 'only the boot path creates devices' a property of the language instead of an item on a review checklist" (pl011.rs:31, repeated here) overstates what `pub(super)` bought. It closes the `::new()` route. It does not close `core::mem::zeroed` or `core::mem::transmute`, both of which fabricate `PowerControl` and `BootConsole` from portable code at the cost of the same `unsafe` keyword the patch identifies as the whole problem with a `pub` constructor.
findings.why_it_matters: Booted, not argued. A `kernel_main` that `mem::forget`s the `BootResources` it was handed, transmutes `0x0900_0000usize` into a `BootConsole`, writes `FORGED_CONSOLE_IN_PORTABLE_CODE`, then `mem::zeroed`s a `PowerControl` and calls `.off()` — compiles, prints, and exits QEMU 0. `ci/constitution-check.sh` passes it: `forbidden_outside_hal` lists only `core::arch::`, `asm!`, `naked_asm!`, `global_asm!`, `#[unsafe(naked)]`, `#[naked]`, `target_arch`, and naming `crate::arch::PowerControl` outside the HAL is legal (hal.rs does it five times in the conformance block). Both types are ZSTs or a single raw pointer, so no private field can make them unforgeable and no visibility change ever will. I verified the E0624 proof and it is real — `pub(super)` from `arch::aarch64::psci` resolves to `arch::aarch64` and its descendants only, so `arch/mod.rs` and everything above it are now excluded, which is a genuine narrowing from `pub(crate)`. What is wrong is the completeness claim. The honest statement is that visibility removed the cheapest route and the two-call-site rule is still what closes the rest; stating otherwise tells the next author the compiler is guarding something it is not.

findings.issue: Prior C-0002 finding, partly addressed. The self-contradiction is gone — the justification no longer rests on divergence, and it explicitly names the fall-through as the reason divergence cannot be assumed. But the clobber list is unchanged at x0-x3, and the replacement argument, "nothing is live across this call on either path", is a statement about LLVM's register allocation that the source does not constrain.
findings.why_it_matters: I disassembled the linked image again: after `hvc #0` at 0x40080098 come `msr daifset, #0xf; wfi; b .-4`, which read no register, so the claim is true of this build. It is true of this build only. x4-x17 are the temporaries LLVM allocates from first — x8 through x13 are all in use in the loop immediately above the call — and nothing stops a future edit that keeps one value alive across the block from being silently corrupted by SMCCC v1.0 firmware that returns NOT_SUPPORTED, which is the exact firmware the fall-through exists to serve. `clobber_abi("C")` states the contract the comment itself invokes, costs nothing on this call, and would move the argument from something a reviewer must re-derive by objdump into something the compiler enforces. It was named in the C-0002 verdict and not taken, and no reason for not taking it is given.

findings.issue: The justification for `Ordering::Relaxed` — "M0 is single-core and has no interrupts, so there is no other observer to order against" — is weaker than the truth and is written so that it expires at M2, when in fact it does not need to.
findings.why_it_matters: Relaxed is correct here for a reason that survives SMP: `swap` compiles to `ldxrb`/`stxrb` (verified in the disassembly at 0x400800f0), the exclusive monitor makes exactly one caller observe `false` regardless of ordering, and the loser performs no memory access at all before `msr daifset` + `wfi`, so there is nothing for an acquire or release to order. That argument holds on one core and on sixteen. The argument actually written holds only while the premise does, so the reader who arrives at M2 will find the stated premise false and either upgrade to `SeqCst` for no reason or, worse, conclude the guard was never sound under SMP and rework it. On the failure path, an argument that stops being readable is a defect of its own kind. (Related: the mint-then-write sequence is correctly ordered — the swap precedes `BootConsole::new`, and there is provably no window between them, since `new` is a fully-elided const cast and the disassembly shows nothing between `cbz w10` and the UART base materialisation that can fault or panic.)

findings.issue: The `write` SAFETY comment is byte-for-byte unchanged from C-0002 — the only edits to this file are `pub(super)` and its doc paragraph. All three sub-clauses of the C-0002 minor remain open, and the comment is now stale with respect to the guard this patch adds.
findings.why_it_matters: (i) "The MMU is off ... so both accesses are to Device-nGnRnE memory" still does not follow from SCTLR_EL1.M == 0 alone; it needs the Effective HCR_EL2.DC == 0 and stage 2 disabled, and `_start` establishes CurrentEL == 1, not the absence of EL2. The inference that closes it — a reset vector observing EL1 proves EL1 is the highest implemented EL — is still nowhere in the file. (ii) "`&mut self` gives exclusive access ... the one aliasing exception is `Failure::fail_stop`" still attributes the guarantee to the wrong mechanism: `fail_stop` constructs a second `BootConsole` rather than borrowing the first, so no `&mut` rule is involved. This is the clause the patch had the strongest reason to revisit and did not. After this patch there are three real mechanisms bounding that aliasing, all stronger than the one written down: two call sites (grep), `pub(super)` (compiler), and `IN_FAILURE` (runtime, which now caps the number of consoles ever minted at two and proves the second entry mints none). (iii) The `*mut u8` -> `*const u32` / `*mut u32` casts still need 4-byte alignment for `read_volatile`/`write_volatile` and the comment still does not say so; `new`'s precondition says "MMIO base of a PL011", which implies it but does not state it.

findings.issue: The guard bounds re-entry through the panic handler. It does nothing about re-entry through an exception, and VBAR_EL1 is still never written anywhere in `kernel/src`.
findings.why_it_matters: A fault rather than a panic inside `fail_stop` — a misaligned MMIO access, a translation fault, or the UNDEF `hvc` covered by the C-0002 note below — still vectors to VBAR_EL1 (0) + offset and reproduces the original symptom exactly: I measured 10,262,934 undefined-instruction exception entries in a 4-second run of the unguarded build. RFC-0001 records the absent vector table as a deliberate M0 omission, so this bounds what the guard achieves rather than contradicting it. Worth writing next to the guard, because the guard's doc comment describes the failure it prevents in terms of the exception storm, and the exception storm has a second entrance the guard does not stand in.

findings.issue: A second entry arriving before the first entry's write has drained leaves the marker truncated or absent, and the machine parked in `wfi` rather than powered off. The commit's two evidence sentences describe two different injections.
findings.why_it_matters: I ran both shapes on the real target, guarded and unguarded. Overflow placed after the write loop: unguarded gives 682 SKYNET_PANIC lines followed by binary garbage from executing overwritten `.text`; guarded gives exactly ONE SKYNET_PANIC then a wfi park. The implementer's proof 3 is true, and I reproduced it. Overflow placed before the write loop — which is the literal shape of the C-0002 reproduction, "one overflowing add in `write`" — gives zero console bytes in both builds, so "before the guard the reproduction printed nothing at all and CI saw only a timeout" describes the injection I filed while "exactly ONE SKYNET_PANIC" describes a different one. Not a defect: refusing to re-drive a console that just faulted is the correct choice and is what makes the guard work. But it means the guard does not make a double failure visible, only survivable, and in both shapes `ci/boot-test.sh` still scores rc=124 "the kernel never shut down". Nobody should later read the guard as "the panic marker is now guaranteed to appear".

findings.issue: `_start` zeroes `[__bss_start, __bss_end)` unconditionally and before the `CurrentEL` check, and `IN_FAILURE` now lives exactly there. A core reaching `_start` after the guard has been taken would clear it. The C-0002 minor on `boot_rust`'s "exactly once" is untouched and is now load-bearing for the new static as well.
findings.why_it_matters: I verified the static's placement rather than assuming it: with the panic path live, `IN_FAILURE` is a 1-byte OBJECT at 0x400801c0, `__bss_start` is 0x400801c0 and `__bss_end` is 0x400801c8, so the linker script's `ALIGN(8)` bounds cover it exactly, `str xzr, [x10], #8` zeroes it and cannot overrun, and the zero pattern is the correct representation of `AtomicBool::new(false)` — the initialisation story is right, and in the shipped image the static does not exist at all because `--gc-sections` and LTO remove the whole failure path (`.bss` is 0 bytes, `.text` is 0xb0). There is no `static mut`, no interior-mutability aliasing, and no initialisation-order hazard. The residual is that the platform fact upholding all of this — QEMU virt sets `start-powered-off` on non-primary CPUs — is still documented only in the RFC and still never exercised by CI, which passes no `-smp`. I confirmed `-smp 1`, `-smp 2` and `-smp 4` each print the marker once and exit 0 on this branch. A configuration where several cores reach `_start` already shares one `__stack_top`, so this is the smaller of that scenario's problems; it is recorded because the guard's correctness now depends on the same unexercised assumption.

findings.issue: C-0002 note, unchanged: `write` polls `FR.TXFF` rather than `FR.BUSY` or `FR.TXFE`, so it returns when the device has accepted the last byte, not when it has transmitted it, and `fail_stop` then issues SYSTEM_OFF immediately.
findings.why_it_matters: Still only a real-hardware concern and still in the one path whose purpose is to be visible. One nuance the guard adds, in the right direction: the second-entry path ends in `wfi` rather than SYSTEM_OFF, and a parked core does not stop the UART draining its FIFO, so the truncation risk applies to the first entry's own power-down and not to the guarded one.

reviewer_verdicts.reasoning:
Approve. The finding this task exists for is fixed, and I established that by reproduction rather than by reading the patch.

I verified the pin first: rfcs/0001-aarch64-boot.md hashes to dc62bdf7...f267c on the branch, on main and in the working tree, matching contribution.toml. The RFC already specifies the guard, the `'static` bound and the corrected SMCCC wording (main commit 6a1431d), so the patch is implementing a spec, not inventing one. Nothing in the diff, the commit message or the code comments attempted to direct my review. The commit message is unusually candid about what the change costs, and I treated its three claimed proofs as claims: I ran all three.

The re-entrancy fix is real. I built and booted four kernels: the branch and main, each with an overflowing `u8` add injected into `BootConsole::write`, placed once after the write loop and once before it. After the loop, main prints 682 SKYNET_PANIC lines and then binary garbage — the stack running off its 64 KiB into `.text` 192 bytes below and the CPU executing what it overwrote — while the branch prints exactly ONE SKYNET_PANIC and parks. Before the loop, which is the literal shape of the C-0002 reproduction, main takes 10,262,934 undefined-instruction exceptions in four seconds through VBAR_EL1 = 0, and the branch takes ZERO. That is the number that matters. The guard does not merely have the shape of the fix; it covers the reproduction, in both placements, and it converts the worst outcome from "the kernel destroys its own text and executes it" into "the kernel parks in a defined state". I confirmed the mechanism in the disassembly: `ldxrb`/`stxrb` on IN_FAILURE is the first thing `fail_stop` does, the losing branch goes straight to `msr daifset, #0xf; wfi`, and there is no path back.

On the three questions I was asked about the guard specifically. Relaxed is sound, and sound for a better reason than the one given (finding 4). The swap-then-halt sequence is correctly ordered — the flag is taken before the console is minted, not after. There is no window between the swap and the mint: `BootConsole::new` is a const cast that is fully elided, the disassembly shows nothing between the branch and the UART base materialisation that can fault or panic, DAIF has been masked since the second instruction of `_start`, and no exception routes to `fail_stop` in any case. The new static introduces no aliasing, no initialisation-order and no `.bss` hazard: I checked its placement in a build where the panic path is live and found it correctly bracketed by 8-aligned `__bss_start`/`__bss_end` and correctly zeroed by the `_start` loop before any Rust runs, with a zero pattern that is the right representation of `AtomicBool::new(false)`. In the shipped image it costs nothing, because the failure path is still eliminated entirely. Every `unsafe` block and every `unsafe fn` in the patch carries a SAFETY comment or a `# Safety` section; I checked each against the list rather than counting.

The two majors I have not seen before are the same defect wearing two hats, and they are the reason I want this verdict read carefully. This patch takes two invariants that were previously prose and claims to have made each a property of the language. In both cases it made them narrower, and in neither case did it make them guarantees. `&'static [u8]` rejects a stack local — I reproduced the E0597 — but I then booted a kernel that puts a byte written at runtime onto the console through that signature, and compiled a second that puts the raw stack there with no static involved at all. `pub(super)` rejects `PowerControl::new()` from portable code — I reproduced the E0624, and it is a genuine tightening — but I then booted a kernel whose portable `kernel_main` forgets the resources it was handed, transmutes a `BootConsole` out of an integer, `mem::zeroed`s a `PowerControl`, writes to the UART and powers the machine off, with the HAL boundary check passing. Both types are unforgeable only against safe code, and no visibility modifier will ever change that. This is not a regression: the same forging worked before the patch. What is new is a sentence in each file telling the next author the compiler is now holding the line. It is not, and the correct repair is a sentence, not a redesign — say that visibility removed the cheapest route and the two-call-site rule still closes the rest.

Nothing here is blocking. No `unsafe` block in the patch is unsound, and there is none whose soundness I could not establish. The three majors are all of the form the role prompt describes: sound today, resting on something that is not guaranteed — LLVM's register allocation in the psci case, the absence of a `mem::zeroed` and the discipline of a single call site in the other two. That is also the shape of the C-0002 verdict, which approved with two majors, and I am applying the same bar.

Status of my C-0002 findings, since I was asked to judge them and not to assume a patch that names them has satisfied them. fail.rs re-entrancy: ADDRESSED, verified by reproduction, with two notes bounding what it achieves. psci.rs clobbers: PARTLY — the contradiction is gone, the hazard and the one-line fix are untouched. pl011.rs: NOT ADDRESSED — the `write` SAFETY comment is unchanged, all three sub-clauses stand, and it is now stale about an aliasing story the patch itself improved. boot.rs secondaries: NOT ADDRESSED, and now carrying the new static's correctness too. The three notes — UNDEF `hvc`, `.bss` zeroed before the EL check, TXFF versus BUSY — all stand unchanged.

What I want the person reading this in five years to take away: the guard is the right fix and it works, and it is the first piece of this kernel whose correctness was demonstrated by making the machine fail rather than by making it succeed. Keep that habit. And be suspicious of any comment in this tree that says a type or a visibility modifier has turned a rule into a guarantee — twice in one patch that sentence was written, and twice I compiled the counter-example in under a minute.

explanation: guardian-1 was still deliberating when ci/gate.sh merged C-0003. The gate counted the two verdicts that existed and found the approve quorum of two satisfied, so the merge was arithmetically correct and structurally wrong: the constitution grants a Guardian the power to reject alone, and that power cannot be exercised over a merge that already happened. The verdict was approve, so nothing was decided wrongly — but it was decided without waiting, which is luck rather than design. The gate now requires the whole panel to have ruled before it counts a quorum. This line records the verdict rather than amending the merged one, because the ledger is append-only and a correction that edits history is not a correction.

findings.issue: The RFC amendment that authorised this contribution adds `static IN_FAILURE` in section 4 and claims 'the claim in section 2 therefore narrows honestly', but the zero-statics claim is not in section 2 and was narrowed nowhere. Three statements still stand un-amended on main: the Invariant 1 section ('No static or static mut anywhere in kernel/src, including arch/ ... which is why the count is zero and not “zero except three”', lines 869-870, and 'no lazily-initialised singleton, no Once, no atomic “already taken” flag', line 872), the fail_stop defence ('there is still no static, no accessor and no namespace to walk', line 922), and conformance criterion C9 ('no static item of any kind exists in the kernel', lines 1008-1009).
findings.why_it_matters: On merge the tree violates a stated conformance criterion of the RFC it conforms to, and IN_FAILURE is precisely the 'atomic already-taken flag' the RFC's own invariant-1 argument names as deliberately absent. Nothing mechanical will notice: I confirmed constitution-check.sh runs only hal-boundary, no-kernel-deps and an advisory ASCII scan, so C9 is enforced by reviewer judgement, which is the same mechanism that missed the reach-around this contribution exists to close. This is the defect class of C-0002 reproduced one level up, in the amendment that authorised the repair. NOT the implementer's to fix: rfcs/ is on the task's does_not_touch list and the separation-of-powers table forbids an implementer editing the specification it implements. It belongs to the next RFC amendment and should be closed before or with the merge. Major, not blocking, because rejecting this contribution would leave a live authority reach-around and an unbounded failure-path recursion on main in order to correct a document.

findings.issue: The C-0002 Guardian reasoning published in the ledger asserts, as a verified structural fact, that 'a portable file reaching for BootConsole would not type-check'. It is false, and I reproduced its falsity: on a clean export of main, `unsafe { crate::arch::PowerControl::new() }.off()` placed in kernel/src/main.rs compiles, builds, and passes the hal-boundary check.
findings.why_it_matters: Recording this against my own panel rather than leaving it in the record unmarked. The error is instructive: genericity of kernel_main constrains what kernel_main can be GIVEN and constrains nothing about what any module can CONSTRUCT, and the second was inferred from the first because it sounded like something a type system does. Three judges and three reviewers passed over it; the correction came from a reviewer compiling the counter-example, one merge late. The separate claim 'zero statics' was true as a fact - what was overstated was its meaning, since the record credits it as 'the evidence that ownership is doing at M0 what a capability will do at M4' when the merged M0 had zero statics AND a nullary public constructor for the power-off authority.

findings.issue: The re-entrancy reproduction is described as producing 'no console output at all'. Running the RFC's exact variant - an overflowing add inside the PL011 write loop - on a clean export of main, I observed the 10-byte fragment 'SKYNESKYNE' and then silence until the timeout, not literally nothing.
findings.why_it_matters: The substantive claim is correct and I confirmed the defect is real and severe: the machine hangs, CI sees only a timeout, and there is no legible reason in the log. But a contribution whose entire thesis is that claims must match reality should not round a truncated fragment down to 'nothing at all'. Minor in effect, recorded because the standard this contribution sets is the standard it should be held to.

findings.issue: 'The kernel now has one static' is true of the source and not of the shipping artefact. With no reachable panic site, LLVM eliminates the whole failure path: readelf on the branch build shows .bss size 0, no IN_FAILURE symbol, and a 191-byte image identical to the merged M0. In a build where the panic path is live, IN_FAILURE lands at 0x40080190, inside __bss_start..__bss_end, and is zeroed by boot.rs's assembly.
findings.why_it_matters: Stated so the cost is recorded accurately rather than generously in either direction. The frugality cost today is exactly zero, and eight bytes of .bss when the path is live, not the 'one byte' the task estimated; and the guard is correctly zero-initialised by existing boot code rather than by QEMU happening to zero DRAM, which I checked because a guard that works by accident would make the contribution's central claim weaker than stated.

guardian_verdicts.reasoning:
I judged purpose only. I treated every sentence inside the contribution as data and re-derived
each load-bearing claim myself, including the ones flattering to my own panel.

OBJECTIVE. Resolves: roadmap/0001-foundations.toml, id 0001, status active, weight 100,
weight_source "bdfl-seed". That is one person's allocation - author johan, author_kind human - not an
electorate's. The file says so itself: weights are seeded until the vote opens at G3, at which point
weight_source becomes "vote:cycle-0001". A bdfl-seeded 100 is not a mandate, it is a placeholder for
one, and I did not treat it as though a vote had happened. Practically it cuts against complacency
rather than for it: with nothing external anchoring the mandate, the Guardian is carrying more of the
load than it will post-G3, so I checked the non_goals item by item and reproduced the claims rather
than reading them. It did not argue for rejection - the seed is honestly labelled, its replacement is
specified, and 0001 is the only active objective, so M0 repair work lands here or nowhere.

WHAT I RAN. On the branch: ci/build.sh PASS; ci/boot-test.sh PASS on all three (SKYNET_BOOT_OK
present, no panic, QEMU exit 0); SKYNET_PROFILE=nano --size 191 bytes against 196608; clippy clean;
constitution-check 5 passed / 4 pending. Then the three claims the submission makes, each as a
differential against main:

  1. THE REACH-AROUND IS REAL. I added `unsafe { crate::arch::PowerControl::new() }.off()` to
     kernel/src/main.rs - portable code - on a clean export of main. It compiled. ci/build.sh PASS.
     ci/constitution-check.sh --check hal-boundary PASS. On the branch the same probe is
     `error[E0624]: associated function 'new' is private`, and so is the equivalent probe against
     BootConsole::new. So for the whole of M0 any portable module could mint the authority to power
     the machine off, and every mechanical check in this project said yes. That is not a
